questions.question: A university's security team is ranking its systems for the move to post-quantum cryptography. Which system should the team put FIRST?

options.A: AES-256 encryption on exam archives kept secret for 30 years
options.B: RSA key exchange on links carrying research data secret for 25 years
options.C: SHA-256 hashes that check the integrity of software downloads
options.D: RSA key exchange on the public course catalog's website

questions.key_concept: Quantum risk is greatest where public-key cryptography protects data that must stay secret for many years.
questions.pre_read: For each system, note two facts: which kind of algorithm protects it, and how long its data must stay secret.
questions.correct_explanation: A large quantum computer could break public-key methods such as RSA, and attackers can record traffic now to decrypt it later. Research data that must stay secret for 25 years and travels under RSA key exchange faces both risks, so it goes first. The AES-256 archive is the runner-up: it is long-lived too, but symmetric encryption with long keys is far less exposed to known quantum attacks.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the archives must stay secret even longer. But AES-256 is symmetric, and long symmetric keys are far less exposed to known quantum attacks than RSA.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because SHA-256 is everywhere. But hash functions are far less exposed to known quantum attacks, and these hashes guard no long-lived secrets.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because RSA is the vulnerable algorithm. But the catalog is public, so recorded traffic holds nothing worth decrypting later.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on hashing, which quantum attacks threaten far less, and D protects public pages with nothing worth recording to decrypt later.
Final two: B beats A because RSA is the quantum-vulnerable algorithm; AES-256 holds up, even for 30-year secrets.
Exam cue: rank post-quantum work by two facts together: a public-key algorithm in use, and how long the data must stay secret.
questions.framework_ref: NIST FIPS 203 Section 1.2 (Context: large-scale quantum computers would put public-key key establishment and signatures at risk); NIST IR 8547 Section 4.1.3 (Symmetric Cryptography: symmetric standards, including hash functions and block ciphers, are significantly less vulnerable to known quantum attacks than public-key standards)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'public-key algorithms protecting long-lived secrets face the greatest quantum risk; symmetric encryption mainly needs long keys' (notes 5.1.7 Quantum-Resistant Cryptography). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Citation update (31 Oct 2026): NIST IR 8547 became final on 27 Oct 2026; the draft citation now points to the final Section 4.1.3.

questions.question: A charity's field investigators use asymmetric encryption to send confidential reports that only the head investigator should be able to read. Which key is MOST appropriate for encrypting each report?

options.A: The sending investigator's own private key
options.B: The sending investigator's own public key
options.C: The head investigator's public key
options.D: A shared copy of the head investigator's private key

questions.key_concept: Asymmetric confidentiality uses the recipient's public key; only the recipient's private key can then decrypt.
questions.pre_read: Ask who must be able to decrypt the report. Then find the key whose partner only that person holds.
questions.correct_explanation: To send a secret with asymmetric encryption, encrypt with the recipient's public key; only the matching private key, which the head investigator alone holds, can decrypt it. The sender's own private key is the runner-up because private keys feel secret, but anyone with the sender's public key could decrypt the report, so it would show who sent it without keeping it confidential.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: private keys are the secret half. But anything encrypted with the sender's private key opens with their public key, which anyone can hold.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because public keys are meant for encrypting. But only the matching private key decrypts, so only the sending investigator could read the report.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it would let the head investigator decrypt. But private keys are never shared; once copied, a private key no longer protects anything.

tips: Eliminate: B locks the report so only its sender can open it, and D copies a private key, which must stay with its owner.
Final two: C beats A because whatever the sender's private key encrypts, their public key opens; secrecy uses the recipient's public key.
Exam cue: for secrecy, encrypt with the recipient's public key. For proof of origin, sign with the sender's private key.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.1 (Data Encryption); NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 (Recommendation for Key Management: Part 1 – General)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'encrypt to someone with their public key; only their private key decrypts' (notes 5.1.5 Symmetric and Asymmetric Encryption). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: An insurance broker approves an enterprise AI assistant for customer data but blocks the free public version of the same chatbot. What should the security analyst tell staff is the MOST important difference?

options.A: The enterprise version makes staff sign in with company accounts
options.B: The enterprise version gives more accurate answers about customer issues
options.C: The enterprise terms require encryption of prompts sent to the provider
options.D: The enterprise terms limit how prompts are kept and reused

questions.key_concept: A prompt is a data transfer; enterprise AI tools are approved for sensitive data because contracts limit how providers keep and reuse prompts.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the two versions share. Then ask what happens to a prompt after it reaches the provider.
questions.correct_explanation: A prompt is a data transfer to the provider. Both versions run the same chatbot, so what makes the enterprise one fit for customer data is its contract, which limits how long prompts are kept and bars training on them; free versions usually lack those limits. Company sign-in is the runner-up: it controls who uses the tool, not what the provider does with the data.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: company sign-in adds accountability and lets IT remove leavers. But it controls who uses the tool, not how the provider keeps or reuses what staff type.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because better answers sound safer. But both versions run the same chatbot, and answer quality says nothing about where customer data goes once typed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because encryption protects data. But the free version also encrypts connections, and that protection ends at the provider, who can still keep the prompt.

tips: Eliminate: B judges the tool by answer quality, and C credits encryption in transit, which both versions use and which ends at the provider.
Final two: D beats A because leakage depends on what the provider may do with prompts; sign-in controls who uses the tool, not where data goes.
Exam cue: a prompt is a data transfer. Whether a tool may take sensitive data depends on what its terms let the provider keep and reuse.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-9 (External System Services); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.10 (Acceptable use of information and other associated assets)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI tools are approved for set classification levels; data above that level needs the policy owner' (notes 5.1.8 Data Leakage into Public AI Services). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): rewritten on the 5.1.8 point (prompts as data transfers under enterprise terms); the data-level lesson repeated cc_d1_019.

questions.question: While building an incident timeline, a ski resort's security analyst finds that the firewall, VPN and server logs disagree by between two and seven minutes for the same events. Which fix BEST prevents this?

options.A: Keep every log for a longer period before deleting it
options.B: Sync every system's clock to one trusted time source
options.C: Convert all log timestamps to the same time zone
options.D: Raise the logging level on each system for more detail

questions.key_concept: Log correlation depends on synchronized clocks; every system should take its time from one trusted source.
questions.pre_read: Notice how big the gap between the logs is. Then ask what kind of problem causes a gap of that size.
questions.correct_explanation: Logs line up only when every system's clock is right, so syncing all clocks to one trusted time source, usually through the Network Time Protocol (NTP), fixes the cause. Converting to one time zone is the runner-up: it removes fixed time-zone offsets, whole or half hours, but these logs differ by a few minutes, which points to drifting clocks that conversion cannot correct.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more history helps investigations. But keeping drifting timestamps for longer does not make them line up.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: mixed time zones do confuse timelines. But zone offsets are fixed, whole or half hours, and these logs disagree by minutes, a sign of drifting clocks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because more detail feels useful. But extra entries carry the same wrong timestamps, so events still cannot be put in order.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps logs longer and D logs more detail, but neither fixes timestamps from clocks that disagree.
Final two: B beats C because a few minutes' difference means drifting clocks; time-zone conversion fixes only fixed zone offsets.
Exam cue: when logs from different systems will not line up, think clock synchronization to one trusted time source.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-45(1) (System Time Synchronization | Synchronization with Authoritative Time Source); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-8 (Time Stamps)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'logs from different systems line up only when every clock syncs to one trusted time source' (notes 5.2.2 Logging and Monitoring). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A payroll officer at a housing charity lets email auto-complete pick an outside address and sends it a spreadsheet of staff bank details. How should the security analyst MOST accurately classify this threat source?

options.A: A malicious insider, because staff data left the organization
options.B: An external threat, since the data reached an outside mail server
options.C: No threat source, because nobody meant to cause any harm
options.D: An accidental insider, since a staff member's mistake caused it

questions.key_concept: Threat sources include accidental human error; insiders can harm the organization by mistake as well as on purpose.
questions.pre_read: Ask who caused the exposure and whether they meant to. Then match those two facts to a threat source.
questions.correct_explanation: Threat sources include accidental ones: people who cause harm through errors in their everyday work. The officer is an insider who exposed data by mistake, so this is an accidental insider threat. No threat source is the runner-up: intent matters when judging adversaries, but accidents still expose data, and risk assessments plan for them too.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because insiders can misuse their access. But malicious means intent, and this was a mistake; labeling it malice would misdirect the response.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the data reached an outsider. But the threat source is whoever caused the exposure, and that was a staff member inside the charity.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: nobody meant harm. But threat sources include accidental human error, and a misdirected email can expose data as badly as an attack.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes intent where there was only a mistake, and B names the recipient, though the error came from inside.
Final two: D beats C because accidental errors are a recognized threat source; harm does not need intent.
Exam cue: insider threats can be deliberate or accidental. Classify by who caused the harm and whether they meant it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Appendix D Table D-2 (Taxonomy of Threat Sources: adversarial, accidental, structural and environmental); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-03 (internal and external threats to the organization are identified and recorded)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'insiders can cause harm by accident as well as on purpose; accidental error is a threat source' (notes 5.2.5 Threat Actors and Motives). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Key letter moved from C to D (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reason clause reworded ('since', no 'data'), matching the distractors' form.

questions.question: At a sector meeting, a partner shares a report marked TLP:RED about attacks on similar firms, and a security analyst who attended wants their IT team to see it. What is the analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Ask the source for permission to share it with the IT team
options.B: Forward it to the IT team, who share the same employer
options.C: Share only the report's indicators with the IT team
options.D: Ask their manager for permission to share it with the IT team

questions.key_concept: TLP labels set how far shared intelligence may travel; TLP:RED stays with the individual recipients unless the source agrees.
questions.pre_read: Note the label on the report and where the analyst wants to send it. Then recall how far that label allows.
questions.correct_explanation: TLP:RED limits a report to the people who received it; at a meeting, that means those present. Only the source, here the partner, can allow wider sharing, so the analyst asks the partner first. Asking a manager is the runner-up: it shows caution, but the label belongs to the source, and no one in the analyst's own firm can widen it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the IT team works for the same firm. But sharing within the organization is what TLP:AMBER allows; TLP:RED stays with the people who received it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because indicators feel like raw data, not the report. But a TLP label covers the information itself, so indicators taken from a TLP:RED report are RED too.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it asks before sharing anything. But only the source can widen a TLP label; a manager in the analyst's own firm has no say over it.

tips: Eliminate: B treats TLP:RED like AMBER, which allows sharing within your organization, and C passes on the report's indicators, but the label covers any part taken from it.
Final two: A beats D because only the source that set a TLP label can widen it; a manager in your own firm has no say over it.
Exam cue: only the source can widen a TLP label. RED is recipients only; AMBER, their organization and clients who need to know; GREEN, their community; CLEAR, anyone.
questions.framework_ref: FIRST Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) v2.0 Section 3a (TLP:RED: for the eyes and ears of individual recipients only); FIRST Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) v2.0 Section 1h (sharing more widely than the label allows needs explicit permission from the source); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-02 (cyber threat intelligence is received from information sharing forums and sources)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'TLP:RED intelligence stays with its individual recipients; wider sharing needs the source' (notes 5.2.6 Cyber Threat Intelligence). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): AMBER now includes clients per TLP v2.0; the key is no longer the only cautious option. Cross-review fixes (31 Oct 2026): D says 'IT staff' so the key no longer ties for longest. Fix round 1 (31 Oct 2026): D is now an in-person briefing with no written copy (the belief that TLP limits only copies) in place of stripping the label, an obvious dishonest act. Fix round 2 (31 Oct 2026): D is now 'ask their manager for permission', a restraint option with the wrong authority, so holding back no longer marks the key; A is reworded in the same form ('ask the source for permission'), so every option names the IT team and the final two turn on who owns the label (TLP v2.0 Sec. 1h). D is the new runner-up; B now falls to the RED/AMBER distinction. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: role junior analyst -> security analyst.

questions.question: On the club laptop, a volunteer installs a photo-resizing tool that works as promised and never spreads to other files or computers, but secretly gives an attacker remote access. Which malware type BEST describes it?

options.A: A worm, because it reached the laptop across a network
options.B: A virus, because it arrived inside a tool the user installed
options.C: Ransomware, because it hands an attacker remote control of the laptop
options.D: A Trojan, because it hid malicious code inside a useful tool

questions.key_concept: A Trojan hides a malicious function inside software the user chooses to install; unlike a virus or worm, it does not copy itself.
questions.pre_read: Note how the tool arrived, whether it spreads to other files or machines, and what it does once inside.
questions.correct_explanation: A Trojan hides a malicious function inside a program the user wants, so the user installs it willingly; here the hidden function is remote access. A virus is the runner-up, since the user did run a program, but a virus copies itself into other files and spreads. This tool never spread; the hidden function inside a useful tool marks it as a Trojan.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the tool came over a network and talks to the attacker. But a worm spreads by itself between machines; here the volunteer chose to install it.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the user did install a program. But a virus copies itself into other files and spreads; this tool never spread to any file or computer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because ransomware is the best-known malware. But ransomware locks files and demands payment; nothing here was encrypted or demanded.

tips: Eliminate: A needs self-spreading with no user action, and C needs locked files and a ransom demand; neither happened here.
Final two: D beats B because the tool hid malicious code and never spread; a virus copies itself into other files.
Exam cue: a virus rides inside other files and spreads, a worm spreads on its own, and a Trojan hides a malicious function in a program the user lets in.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1 Section 2.1 (Forms of Malware: viruses, worms and Trojan horses)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a Trojan poses as useful software the user installs and does not replicate' (notes 5.2.8 Malware Basics). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review fixes (31 Oct 2026): C gains 'remote' so the key no longer ties for longest. Fix round 1 (31 Oct 2026): stem says the tool 'never spreads to other files or computers' in place of the awkward 'copies itself nowhere' (with 'club volunteer' and 'gives an attacker remote access' to stay within 35 words); explanations match. Fix round 2 (31 Oct 2026): the stem now names the club laptop that A and C refer to (kept to two sentences and 35 words by moving the laptop to the front and asking which malware type fits); D says the tool hid malicious code inside a useful tool, matching 'works as promised' and SP 800-83r1's 'hidden malicious purpose'.

questions.question: A security operations center (SOC) analyst finds a staff member's current password posted on a public paste site, though logs show no one has used it yet. How should the analyst MOST accurately classify this?

options.A: An ordinary event, since no login has used the password yet
options.B: An incident, since the leak imminently threatens the account
options.C: A false positive, since the account's logs show no misuse
options.D: Not a security matter, since the leak happened on an outside site

questions.key_concept: An incident includes imminent threats to confidentiality, integrity or availability, not only harm that has already occurred.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether harm must already have happened for something to count as an incident. Then recall the definition.
questions.correct_explanation: An incident covers occurrences that actually or imminently threaten confidentiality, integrity or availability. A working password in public hands lets anyone sign in at any moment, so this meets the definition, and the analyst escalates it as the plan requires. An ordinary event is the runner-up: nothing has been misused yet, but waiting for the first login would let the harm happen first.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: no one has signed in with it yet. But incidents include imminent threats, and a working password in public can be used at any moment.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the account looks clean. But a false positive is an alert on normal activity; a real password on a public site is a genuine finding.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the paste site is outside the organization's systems. But the exposed password opens the organization's own account, wherever it was posted.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a genuine finding as a false alarm, and D treats an outside website as beyond security, though the password opens an internal account.
Final two: B beats A because incidents include imminent threats; a usable password in public does not need a login first.
Exam cue: incidents cover harm that has happened and harm that is about to. Exposed working credentials count.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Section 1 (Introduction: events, adverse events and incidents); NIST CSF 2.0 DE.AE-08 (incidents are declared when adverse events meet the defined incident criteria)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'incidents include imminent threats, not only harm that has already occurred' (notes 5.2.1 Events, Alerts and Incidents). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review fixes (31 Oct 2026): stem spells out security operations center (SOC).

questions.question: A small security operations center (SOC) faces thousands of alerts a day, mostly duplicates, and analysts have started missing real attacks. Which change is BEST for the SOC lead to make?

options.A: Add AI correlation that groups related alerts into cases to review
options.B: Switch off the half of the detection rules that alert most often
options.C: Let an AI tool close the alerts it rates as harmless
options.D: Have analysts work through alerts strictly in the order they arrive

questions.key_concept: AI correlation reduces alert fatigue by grouping and ranking alerts, while analysts keep the decision to close or escalate.
questions.pre_read: Name the cause of the missed attacks. Then ask which option reduces the noise without removing human judgment.
questions.correct_explanation: Alert fatigue comes from volume and duplicates, so AI correlation that groups related alerts into ranked cases shrinks the queue while analysts still judge each case. Letting the AI close alerts it rates harmless is the runner-up: it cuts the queue further, but models make mistakes, and auto-closing with no analyst check turns those mistakes into missed attacks.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because noisy rules cause the flood. But switching rules off creates blind spots; noisy rules are tuned so they fire less on normal activity.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it shrinks the queue the most. But models can be wrong, and alerts closed with no analyst check become attacks nobody sees.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it feels fair and thorough. But arrival order ignores impact, and the queue stays just as long, so real attacks still wait behind noise.

tips: Eliminate: B creates blind spots by disabling detection, and D keeps the same flood, ordered by arrival time instead of impact.
Final two: A beats C because AI should shrink the queue while people keep the decisions; unreviewed auto-closing hides the model's mistakes.
Exam cue: in a SOC, AI groups, ranks and summarizes alerts; people stay accountable for closing and escalating them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 DE.AE-03 (information is correlated from multiple sources); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 3.2 (roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems are defined)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI correlation shrinks the alert queue while analysts keep the decisions' (notes 5.2.4 AI-Driven Correlation and Alert Fatigue). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 5.3 Incident response. Response plan and team
questions.question: During a suspected compromise of a city library network's email server, the incident response lead must coordinate the team. Which channel is BEST for the lead to use?

options.A: Library email, the plan's usual channel, with messages marked confidential
options.B: The library's chat tool, which signs in with email accounts
options.C: A group chat channel on the staff members' personal messaging apps
options.D: A conference phone bridge the plan names as its backup channel

questions.key_concept: Incident plans name out-of-band channels in advance, so responders can coordinate if normal systems are compromised.
questions.pre_read: Ask which systems the attacker might already control. Then find the channel that is both separate and approved.
questions.correct_explanation: If attackers may control email, anything sent through it, or through tools tied to its accounts, could be read. The phone bridge the plan names as its backup is out-of-band: it runs apart from those systems, keeps coordination private and is already approved. Personal messaging apps are the runner-up: they are separate from the email server, but they are unapproved and put incident details outside the organization's control.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the plan makes email the usual channel. But attackers who control the server can read messages whatever label they carry.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because chat feels separate from email. But it signs in with the same accounts, so a compromise of email identities may reach it too.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: these apps are separate from the email server. But they are unapproved, and incident details would sit on personal accounts outside the organization's control.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on the email server under suspicion, and B depends on the same email accounts, so both may be watched.
Final two: D beats C because the plan's phone bridge is out-of-band and approved; personal apps put incident data outside the organization's control.
Exam cue: when the normal channel may be compromised, use the out-of-band channel the plan names in advance.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-37 (Out-of-band Channels); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-8 (Incident Response Plan)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'plans set up out-of-band channels in advance for when normal systems may be compromised' (notes 5.3.1 The Incident Response Plan and Team). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review fixes (31 Oct 2026): C gains 'the' so the key no longer ties for longest. Fix round 1 (31 Oct 2026): stem grammar fixed ('Which channel is BEST for the lead to use?'); D names a planned phone bridge instead of spelling out 'separate out-of-band channel', so the tested term no longer sits only in the key. Fix round 2 (31 Oct 2026): A now cites the plan as well ('the plan's usual channel'), so 'plan' no longer sits only on the key; D says the plan names the bridge as its backup channel (plans name channels, they do not set them up), and at 62 characters it is no longer the clear odd-one-short option.

questions.question: After a contained ransomware outbreak at a furniture maker, a department head wants the lessons learned review to focus on the technician who missed a patch. Which approach is BEST for the incident response lead?

options.A: Name the technician as the root cause in the review's findings
options.B: Cancel the review and close the case, as it was quickly contained
options.C: Assign owned fixes for the gaps that let the patch go unnoticed
options.D: Make retraining that technician the review's main corrective action

questions.key_concept: Lessons learned reviews are blameless: they look for process, tool and training gaps and give each fix an owner.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the review is for: finding someone to blame, or stopping the next incident. Then judge each option.
questions.correct_explanation: A lessons learned review is blameless: it asks why one missed patch could go unnoticed, such as gaps in patch tracking, asset records or monitoring, and gives each fix an owner and a deadline. Retraining the technician is the runner-up: skills matter, but it treats one person as the whole problem and leaves open the gaps that let a single miss cause an outbreak.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the missed patch let the attack in. But naming individuals makes people hide mistakes, and the real causes usually lie in process and controls.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the incident ended quickly. But small incidents still expose gaps, and reviewing them costs less than learning the same lesson from a bigger one.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: training can prevent repeat misses. But focusing on one person leaves the tracking and monitoring gaps that let one missed patch go unnoticed.

tips: Eliminate: A pins the cause on one person, which discourages honest reporting, and B skips a review because the incident was small.
Final two: C beats D because a review fixes the system that let one miss go unnoticed; retraining one person leaves those gaps open.
Exam cue: lessons learned reviews are blameless and end with owned, dated actions on process, tools and training.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.IM-03 (improvements are identified from execution of operational processes, procedures, and activities); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'lessons learned reviews are blameless and assign owned fixes to process, tool and training gaps' (notes 5.3.6 Lessons Learned and Continuous Improvement). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. questions.question: A hospital's incident response lead wants to confirm on-call responders can actually carry out the ransomware playbook's isolation steps within 30 minutes, without touching live systems. Which exercise fits this goal BEST?

options.A: A tabletop exercise in which the team talks through the steps
options.B: A functional exercise performing the steps on a simulated network
options.C: A drill in which staff phone everyone on the contact list
options.D: A read-through of the written ransomware playbook by the team

questions.key_concept: Tabletop exercises test roles and decisions by discussion; proving people can perform steps in time needs a hands-on functional exercise.
questions.pre_read: Notice what must be shown: people performing steps, and a time limit. Ask which exercises have people act rather than talk.
questions.correct_explanation: Only a hands-on exercise shows whether responders can perform the isolation steps and how long they take. In a functional exercise, responders carry out their roles in a simulated environment, so the time is measured without touching live systems. The tabletop is the runner-up: it is the best-known exercise and checks roles and decisions, but it is discussion only, so no step is performed or timed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a tabletop checks who does what. But it is discussion only; nobody performs the steps, so it cannot show they take under 30 minutes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because drills are hands-on. But calling the contact list tests whether people can be reached, not whether they can isolate systems.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the playbook must be right. But reading it checks the document, not whether responders can carry out its steps in time.

tips: Eliminate: C practices a different task, and D checks a document; neither has responders perform the isolation steps or measures time.
Final two: B beats A because a tabletop only discusses the steps; a functional exercise has responders perform and time them.
Exam cue: talk-through exercises test roles and decisions. To prove people can act within a time, choose a hands-on exercise.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-84 Section 4 (Tabletop Exercises: discussion-based events); NIST SP 800-84 Section 5 (Functional Exercises: performing duties in a simulated operational environment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'tabletops test decisions by discussion; proving a capability or time needs a hands-on exercise' (notes 5.3.7 Incident Response Exercises and Tabletops). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): a timed restore is a test under SP 800-84, so the item moved to an IR functional exercise; it also repeated cc_d2_009.

questions.question: Midway through a weeks-long incident, a security analyst finds that a detection rule missed the attacker's first step. Under NIST SP 800-61r3, what is the BEST way to handle this lesson?

options.A: Share it now with the detection team through the response lead
options.B: Hold it for the lessons learned meeting once recovery ends
options.C: Record it as the incident's root cause and close the analysis
options.D: Fix the detection rule themselves straight away in the live system

questions.key_concept: NIST's CSF 2.0-based model treats improvement as continuous: lessons are shared when found, not only after recovery.
questions.pre_read: Notice when the lesson appears and how long the incident has left to run. Then ask when it should reach its owner.
questions.correct_explanation: Current NIST guidance treats improvement as continuous: lessons should be shared as soon as they are found, not held until recovery ends. A detection gap could hide the attacker's next move, so passing it to the detection team through the response lead helps now. Holding it for the final meeting is the runner-up: that is the older model's timing, and the gap would stay open for weeks.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the older lifecycle collected lessons at the end. But current NIST guidance shares lessons as soon as they are found, and this gap matters now.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the miss feels central. But a missed detection explains why the attack went unseen, not how it got in, and analysis is still under way.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a quick fix seems helpful. But detection rules belong to their owners and change through approval; an unreviewed edit could break other detections.

tips: Eliminate: C mistakes a detection gap for the root cause and ends analysis early, and D changes another team's rule without approval.
Final two: A beats B because SP 800-61r3 shares lessons when found; waiting leaves the gap open for weeks.
Exam cue: under SP 800-61r3, improvement never stops. Share a lesson through the right owner as soon as you find it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Section 2.1 (Incident Response Life Cycle Model: lessons learned are shared as soon as they are identified); NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Table 1 (Previous incident response life cycle model's phases and corresponding CSF 2.0 Functions)

questions.question: A staff email account at a print shop is sending phishing messages to coworkers, and the playbook lets the on-call analyst disable accounts that send malicious mail. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Email all staff, warning them not to open the messages
options.B: Disable the email service for everyone until the investigation ends
options.C: Delete the phishing messages it sent from every coworker's mailbox
options.D: Disable the account that is sending the phishing messages

questions.key_concept: Containment stops the spread at its source first; clean-up and eradication follow under the incident response lead.
questions.pre_read: Find the source of the spread and what the playbook lets the analyst do. Then pick the step that stops the source.
questions.correct_explanation: Containment comes first, and the playbook gives the analyst authority to disable accounts, so disabling the sending account stops new phishing at its source; the incident response lead then directs the rest. Deleting the messages is the runner-up: it cleans up what was already sent, but the account keeps sending more while it stays active.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because warning people feels protective. But the account keeps sending, and incident messages to all staff come from the roles the plan names.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it would stop all phishing at once. But it halts every user's email when one account is the problem, a decision for management.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: removing the messages protects coworkers. But it is clean-up, not containment; while the account stays active, it keeps sending new ones.

tips: Eliminate: A warns staff while the source keeps sending, and B shuts down everyone's email, which is wider than needed and not the analyst's call.
Final two: D beats C because containment stops the source; deleting messages cleans up while new ones keep arriving.
Exam cue: contain before you clean up. When the playbook gives you the containment step, take it and report at once.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.MI-01 (incidents are contained); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'containment stops the source first; clean-up follows under the incident response lead' (notes 5.3.3 Containment, Eradication and Recovery). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A marketing team pays for an outside AI image service with a company card and uploads product photos to it. Which step is BEST for the system administrator who learns of it?

options.A: Block the AI service's website at the web proxy straight away
options.B: Leave it out, since the inventory tracks company-owned hardware only
options.C: Record the AI service in the inventory under an accountable owner
options.D: Leave tracking to the provider, which owns the systems

questions.key_concept: Asset inventories include outside services and AI tools, each with a named owner; unknown assets are recorded before any removal decision.
questions.pre_read: Ask what belongs in an asset inventory and who decides what happens to an asset. Then judge each option.
questions.correct_explanation: An inventory covers every asset the organization relies on, including outside services and AI tools, and each needs a named owner who is accountable for its use. Recording the service and confirming its owner brings it under management, so the owner can take it through the AI approval route. Blocking it is the runner-up: unknown services are a risk, but blocking is decided through the AI approval route, not by an administrator acting alone.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: unapproved services carry risk. But blocking a service the business relies on is decided through the AI approval route, not by a system administrator alone.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because hardware is the classic inventory. But inventories also cover software, outside services and AI tools, or unknown services go unmanaged.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the provider runs the service. But the provider does not know what the organization uploads; tracking its own use stays with the organization.

tips: Eliminate: B limits the inventory to hardware, and D hands tracking to the provider; inventories cover the services and AI tools the organization uses.
Final two: C beats A because unknown assets are recorded and given an owner first; blocking is decided through the approval route, not by a lone administrator.
Exam cue: found something unknown? Record it and find its owner, who takes it through approval, before anyone blocks, unplugs or ignores it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-04 (inventories of services provided by suppliers are maintained); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.6 (mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'inventories cover outside services and AI tools, each with a named owner' (notes 5.4.1 Asset Inventory and Ownership). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review fixes (31 Oct 2026): blocking is now decided through the AI approval route (the owner is accountable for the use), agreeing with cc_d2_004 and cc_d4_019; key unchanged. questions.question: A hotel group's procurement team will buy 300 smart room thermostats next month and plans to involve IT security after installation. What should the IT security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Write requirements, including patch support, into the purchase
options.B: Harden each thermostat to the secure baseline once it is installed
options.C: Pick the cheapest model and replace any that later prove insecure
options.D: Keep each thermostat's factory settings, such as its admin password

questions.key_concept: Security requirements, such as vendor patch support, belong in the acquisition stage, before any model is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Notice when IT security is due to get involved. Ask what can still be changed after the devices are bought.
questions.correct_explanation: Security belongs in the asset lifecycle from acquisition: requirements such as ongoing patch support, changeable default passwords and encryption should decide which model is bought. Hardening after installation is the runner-up: it is good practice, but it cannot add patch support or settings a model lacks, so 300 weak devices could be locked in for years.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: hardening to a baseline is good practice. But it cannot add patch support or settings a model lacks; those must be required before purchase.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it saves money now. But replacing insecure devices later costs more and leaves weak devices on the network until then.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because factory settings work out of the box. But defaults favor easy setup over security, and default admin passwords are published for anyone to try.

tips: Eliminate: C buys first and fixes later, and D keeps factory defaults, which favor easy setup over security.
Final two: A beats B because hardening cannot add what a model lacks; requirements must shape the purchase.
Exam cue: security starts at acquisition. Requirements set before buying cost less than fixes after installation.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-4 (Acquisition Process); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-08 (systems, hardware, software, services, and data are managed throughout their life cycles)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'security requirements belong in acquisition, before a model is chosen' (notes 5.4.2 The Asset Lifecycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review fixes (31 Oct 2026): stem says 'propose' instead of 'recommend', keeping the practitioner voice. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'such'; distractor D reworded (no 'since'/'is', now 'such as').

questions.question: A drift scan flags that 15 file servers now run a backup agent missing from their secure baseline, and an approved change request installed it last week. What is the system administrator's BEST next step?

options.A: Remove the agent from all 15 servers to match the baseline again
options.B: Update the baseline through change management to add the agent
options.C: Turn off drift scanning on those servers to stop the repeat alerts
options.D: Report the agent as an unauthorized change and possible incident

questions.key_concept: Baselines change only through change management; an approved change that adds a component means the baseline must be updated.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the difference from the baseline was approved. Then ask which record is now out of date.
questions.correct_explanation: Drift is a difference from the baseline, but this one came from an approved change, so the baseline itself is now out of date. Updating it through change management makes it match the approved state, so future scans and new builds include the agent. Removing the agent is the runner-up: it restores the old baseline, but it undoes an approved change and stops the backups it provides.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: returning drift to the baseline is the usual fix. But this difference was approved; removing it undoes a sanctioned change and stops the backups.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the alerts are noise right now. But switching off drift checks hides every future change on those servers, approved or not.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because unapproved changes are treated as possible incidents. But this change has an approved request, so it is not unauthorized.

tips: Eliminate: C blinds the drift check, and D treats a change with an approved request as unauthorized.
Final two: B beats A because an approved change means the baseline is stale; update the baseline instead of undoing the change.

Exam cue: for any drift, ask first whether it was approved. Approved changes update the baseline; unapproved ones are restored by the system's maintainer, or reported as possible incidents when unexplained and risky.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-2 (Baseline Configuration); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an approved change that adds a component means the baseline is updated through change management' (notes 5.4.4 Configuration Management and Secure Baselines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review fixes (31 Oct 2026): exam cue now says who restores unapproved drift and when it is reported instead, agreeing with cc_d5_041 and cc_d2_003; actor renamed to the canonical 'system administrator'; key unchanged.

questions.question: A security analyst's weekly review finds a new firewall rule, with no change request, allowing internet access to the payroll database on a firewall the network team runs. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Delete the rule at once to restore the approved configuration
options.B: Report it as a possible incident for responders to handle
options.C: Leave it, since a senior engineer probably added it for a reason
options.D: File a change request now so the rule is approved retroactively

questions.key_concept: An unexplained change that opens a serious exposure is a possible incident; if you do not run the system, report it instead of undoing it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an unexplained change could mean, and who runs the firewall. Then decide what the analyst's role allows.
questions.correct_explanation: A change with no approval is treated as a possible incident until explained, and a rule opening the payroll database to the internet could be an intruder's work. Reporting it starts the response, and the firewall's owners and responders decide on containment. Deleting the rule is the runner-up: it closes the exposure, but the analyst does not run the firewall, and deleting it alters the evidence responders need to trace who added it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the rule is risky and should not stay. But the network team runs the firewall, and deleting the rule alone alters evidence responders need to trace it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because senior staff do make quick fixes. But unapproved changes are treated as possible incidents until explained, whoever may have made them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because change requests fix missing paperwork. But approving an unexplained rule after the fact could legitimize an intruder's change.

tips: Eliminate: D approves an unexplained change after the fact, and C assumes good intent without checking.
Final two: B beats A because an unexplained rule exposing payroll data is a possible incident, on a firewall the analyst doesn't run; owners and responders decide containment.
Exam cue: an unexplained change that opens a path to sensitive data is a possible incident. On a system you don't run, report it; don't quietly undo it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 6.8 (Information security event reporting)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an unapproved change is a possible incident until explained; report it instead of quietly undoing it' (notes 5.4.6 Change Management). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Fix round 1 (31 Oct 2026): Final two now gives the two deciding facts (unexplained and risky; a firewall the analyst does not run) instead of a blanket rule, agreeing with cc_d5_040. Key letter moved from D to B (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged.

questions.question: During threat modeling of a ticket-booking app, a security analyst notes that a user could edit the price field in a request before it reaches the server. Which STRIDE category does this MOST accurately fit?

options.A: Spoofing, since the user poses as someone else
options.B: Tampering, since data is changed without permission
options.C: Repudiation, since the user could later deny the change
options.D: Elevation of privilege, since the user gains extra rights

questions.key_concept: STRIDE names six threat types; changing data without permission is tampering, a threat to integrity.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the user actually changes: their identity, their rights or the data. Then match it to a category.
questions.correct_explanation: Tampering is changing data or code without permission, a threat to integrity, and editing the price in a request is exactly that; the design fix is for the server to set or check prices itself. Elevation of privilege is the runner-up because the user gets a better deal, but their rights never change: they act as the same ordinary customer.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because attackers often fake identities. But the user acts as themselves; nothing here involves posing as another person or system.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because disputes over prices can follow. But repudiation is denying an action when there is no proof; the threat here is the changed data itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the user gains an advantage. But their rights stay the same; changing a value they should not control is tampering with data.

tips: Eliminate: A needs someone posing as another identity, and C is about denying actions later; neither describes an edited price.
Final two: B beats D because the user's rights never change; they alter data, which is tampering.
Exam cue: in STRIDE, ask what is violated: identity, data, proof of actions, secrecy, uptime or rights.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet (Threat Identification: STRIDE categories); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-11(2) (Developer Testing and Evaluation | Threat Modeling and Vulnerability Analyses)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'STRIDE names six threat types; changing data without permission is tampering' (notes 5.5.4 Threat Modeling). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: role junior analyst -> security analyst.

questions.question: During a tailgating test the client approved at a garden-supply wholesaler, a staff member grabs the arm of the tester posing as a courier, and others gather angrily. What should the tester do FIRST?

options.A: Keep up the courier story to see whether staff follow procedure
options.B: Ask to be walked to reception, still posing as the delivery courier
options.C: Stop the test, say who they are and show the authorization letter
options.D: End the test by pulling free and leaving by the nearest exit

questions.key_concept: Physical testers stop when anyone's safety is at risk and show their authorization letter, so staff can confirm the test through a known contact.
questions.pre_read: Notice what has just changed in the situation. Then ask what matters more than finishing the test.
questions.correct_explanation: People's safety outranks any test result, so once a confrontation turns physical, the tester stops, identifies themselves and shows the signed authorization letter, so staff can confirm the test through the security team's known contact rather than the tester's word. Leaving at once is the runner-up: it ends the pretext, but pulling free can escalate a struggle, and staff are left believing a real intruder escaped.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the test is meant to be realistic. But realism never outweighs safety; once someone grabs the tester, the test has to stop.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reception is a calmer place. But keeping the pretext while staff are angry prolongs the danger; the letter exists for this moment.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it ends the confrontation quickly. But pulling free can turn into a struggle, and staff may chase or call police, believing a real intruder got away.

tips: Eliminate: A and B both keep the pretext going after the confrontation turned physical, when safety should end the test.
Final two: C beats D because revealing the role and letter calms the situation; fleeing can escalate it and leaves staff alarmed.
Exam cue: people come first. In any test or response, stop when someone could be hurt, and use the agreed way to verify.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-115 Section 5.2 (Penetration Testing: security guards should be made aware of how to verify the validity of tester activity); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-8 (Penetration Testing)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'physical testers stop when safety is at risk and use their authorization letter so staff can verify' (notes 5.5.5 Physical and Social Engineering Penetration Tests). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review fixes (31 Oct 2026): the letter lets staff confirm the test through the security team's known contact, and the SP 800-115 Section 5.2 citation uses the same form as cc_d5_065.

questions.subtopic: 5.5 Security testing. Scanning and penetration testing
questions.question: A database owner approved monthly vulnerability scans, and the latest one flags a critical flaw that a security analyst wants to exploit to prove it is real. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Get the owner's written approval for a scoped penetration test
options.B: Exploit it now, since the owner already approved the monthly scanning
options.C: Patch the flaw right away and close the scan finding
options.D: Treat it as a false positive unless a second scanner agrees

questions.key_concept: Scanning and exploitation are different activities; each needs the system owner's approval for that type and level of testing.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the owner approved with what the analyst now wants to do. Ask whether one covers the other.
questions.correct_explanation: A scan identifies known weaknesses; exploiting one is penetration testing, which needs separate written approval and agreed scope from the system owner. Asking also tells the owner about the critical flaw. Exploiting under the scanning approval is the runner-up: it seems covered, but approval is for a specific type and level of testing, and an exploit can crash a production database.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the owner did approve testing of a kind. But scanning looks for flaws, and exploiting one is a different, riskier activity the approval does not cover.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because critical flaws need fixing fast. But the database belongs to its owner, and changing it skips change management; report the finding and let the owner decide.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because scanners do produce false positives. But a critical finding is validated and reported to the owner, not dismissed for lack of a second tool.

tips: Eliminate: C changes the owner's database without change management, and D dismisses a critical finding instead of validating and reporting it.
Final two: A beats B because approval covers a type and level of testing; scanning approval does not cover exploitation.
Exam cue: a scan finds weaknesses; a penetration test exploits them. Each needs the owner's approval for that specific activity.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-115 Section 6.5 (Assessment Plan Development: the plan states the type and level of testing permitted); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-8 (Penetration Testing)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'scanning and exploitation are different activities, each needing its own approval from the owner' (notes 5.5.2 Vulnerability Scanning and Penetration Testing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review fixes (31 Oct 2026): B gains 'monthly' so the key is no longer the longest option. Fix round 1 (31 Oct 2026): C opens 'Run the exploit' so B and C no longer share an opener that lets them fall as a pair. Fix round 2 (31 Oct 2026): C is now an unapproved patch (the fix-it-yourself reflex) in place of running the exploit at night, which was close to a strawman and fell together with B. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'; distractor C given 'and', no 'since'; role junior analyst -> security analyst.

questions.question: An authorized test shows a crafted message tricks a customer help desk chatbot into revealing internal staff phone numbers that customers never get. Which fix should the security analyst propose as BEST before retesting?

options.A: Add 'never reveal internal data' to the chatbot's instructions
options.B: Retrain the chatbot on a larger set of help desk chats
options.C: Accept the finding, since phone numbers are rarely sensitive data
options.D: Remove the chatbot's access to data it does not need

questions.key_concept: Models stay open to prompt injection, so limit the data and actions an AI tool can reach instead of relying on instructions.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the chatbot could be tricked again after each fix. Then pick the fix that still works if it is.
questions.correct_explanation: Current models remain open to prompt injection, so the strongest fix assumes the chatbot can be tricked and limits what it can reach: if it cannot access staff numbers, no message can extract them. Adding a 'never reveal' instruction is the runner-up: it may block some attempts, but instructions share the input stream attackers manipulate, and crafted messages often override them.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: clear instructions can block some attempts. But attackers craft input to override instructions, so the data stays reachable whenever a trick succeeds.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more training sounds like better behavior. But extra help desk chats do not teach the model to resist crafted attacks, and the data stays reachable.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because phone numbers seem low risk. But internal contact lists fuel phishing, and accepting a risk is the owner's decision, not the analyst's.

tips: Eliminate: B adds training data that does nothing against manipulation, and C accepts a risk the analyst does not own.
Final two: D beats A because a chatbot that cannot reach the data cannot leak it; instructions can be talked around.
Exam cue: assume an AI tool can be tricked. Limit what it can access and do, then retest.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 3.3.3 (Mitigations for direct prompting attacks: design systems assuming a model with access to sensitive data may leak it); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'models stay open to prompt injection, so limit what an AI tool can reach instead of relying on instructions' (notes 5.5.6 Testing AI-Integrated Defenses). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-review fixes (31 Oct 2026): stem says 'propose' instead of 'recommend', keeping the practitioner voice.

questions.question: A software firm's order system swaps card numbers for random tokens issued by a token vault. To keep the card numbers safe, which component should the security analyst rate MOST in need of protection?

options.A: The order database, which now stores a token for every card
options.B: The support screens, which show each order's token
options.C: The vault's access log, which records every token lookup made
options.D: The vault, which holds the mapping behind every token

questions.key_concept: Tokens are worthless alone, so tokenization moves the risk into the vault, the one place that maps tokens back to real values.
questions.pre_read: For each component, ask what an attacker who stole it could actually recover.
questions.correct_explanation: Tokens have no mathematical link to the card numbers, so the database, screens and log hold no card number an attacker could recover. The vault alone turns tokens back into real numbers, so it needs the strongest protection. The order database is the runner-up: it is the main business system, but after tokenization it holds only tokens.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it is the main business system. But after tokenization it stores only tokens, which are useless without the vault that maps them back.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because staff see data on screens. But the screens show only tokens, which reveal no card number to anyone who reads them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because logs can leak details. But this log records that lookups happened, not the card numbers; only the vault holds those.

tips: Eliminate: B shows only tokens, and C records that lookups happened, not card numbers; neither holds a card number an attacker could steal.
Final two: D beats A because only the vault turns tokens back into card numbers; the order database now holds only tokens.
Exam cue: tokenization concentrates the risk. Find the one place that maps tokens back to real values, and protect it most.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-188 Section 4.3.1 (Removing or Transforming of Direct Identifiers: random pseudonyms through a protected lookup table)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'tokenization moves the risk into the vault, the one place that maps tokens back to real values' (notes 5.1.3 Data Masking and Tokenization). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A tea importer's payroll server has a failed solid-state drive that will not power on, and the vendor's warranty swap keeps the faulty drive. Which sanitization step is BEST for the system administrator?

options.A: Send the drive back, since a dead drive cannot be read
options.B: Keep the drive and purge it with its built-in sanitize command
options.C: Return the drive with a written request that the vendor wipe it
options.D: Hold the drive back from the vendor for destruction

questions.key_concept: Media that cannot be purged, such as a failed drive, is destroyed before it can leave the organization's control.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether a drive that will not power on still holds readable data, and who controls it once it is shipped.
questions.correct_explanation: A drive that will not power on cannot run a purge command, yet its memory chips can still be read in a lab, and a warranty swap puts it outside the organization's control for good. Destruction is the method left, recorded by serial number. Asking the vendor to wipe it is the runner-up: it sounds responsible, but unsanitized payroll data leaves your control on a promise you cannot verify.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the drive seems dead. But laboratory tools can read flash chips directly, so the payroll data stays recoverable once the drive leaves.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a built-in sanitize command is the usual purge for solid-state drives. But the drive's own controller must run it, and a drive that will not power on cannot.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the vendor may well wipe returned drives. But the data leaves unsanitized, on a promise you cannot verify, so destruction is the safer method.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a dead drive cannot be read, and B relies on a sanitize command that a drive which will not power on cannot run.
Final two: D beats C because destruction sanitizes the drive while it is still in your control; a vendor's promise to wipe it cannot be verified.
Exam cue: when media cannot be purged, destroy it before it leaves your control, and record it. Deleting, formatting and promises are not sanitization.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 Section 3.1.3 (Destroy Sanitization Method: destruction may be the only option when the media fails); NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 Section 4.3.4 (Control of Media: media exchanged for warranty and not returned is out of organizational control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'media that cannot be purged and will leave the organization's control is destroyed and recorded' (notes 5.1.4 Media Sanitization: Clear, Purge and Destroy). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'; role IT technician -> system administrator. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key names the vendor, so 'vendor' is no longer on a distractor only.

questions.question: A help desk analyst at a shipping company is explaining website certificates to new staff. What does a trusted certificate authority's signature on a site's certificate MOST directly assure?

options.A: The site's code has been checked and is free of known flaws
options.B: The site's owner has been vetted as honest and safe to pay
options.C: The public key in the certificate belongs to the named site
options.D: Traffic to the site is encrypted with the certificate authority's key

questions.key_concept: A certificate authority's signature binds a public key to its named owner; it says nothing about the owner's honesty or the site's code.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a certificate authority actually checks before it signs, and what it never checks.
questions.correct_explanation: A certificate binds a public key to its owner: the certificate authority verifies that the named party controls the key, then signs, so a browser can trust it is talking to the real site. The vetted-owner option is the runner-up: verification checks identity and control of the name, not honesty, so a fraudster can hold a valid certificate for their own look-alike site.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a valid certificate feels like a safety seal. But certificate authorities check identity, not code; a certified site can still have serious flaws.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the authority does verify who the owner is. But identity is not honesty, and criminals can obtain valid certificates for their own look-alike sites.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because certificates enable encryption. But the session uses keys agreed with the site; the authority's private key only signs certificates.

tips: Eliminate: A expects certificates to test code, and D puts the authority's key into the traffic; certificates do neither.
Final two: C beats B because a certificate proves who holds the key, not whether they are honest; criminals can get valid certificates too.
Exam cue: a certificate answers 'is this key really theirs?' It does not answer 'are they trustworthy?' or 'is their software safe?'
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 Section 2.1 (Glossary: a public-key certificate is signed by a trusted party, binding the public key to the entity); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.3.2 (Public Key Electronic Signatures: anyone can verify with the signer's public key)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a certificate authority's signature binds a public key to its owner, not to the owner's honesty' (notes 5.1.6 Hashing, Digital Signatures and Certificates). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Key letter moved from B to C (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged.

questions.question: A runbook has analysts open an incident ticket when logs stop for an hour; the payroll server's three-hour silence has no change record, and its system owner blames maintenance. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Hold the incident ticket until the owner confirms the maintenance
options.B: Restart the logging agent and close the alert
options.C: Raise the incident ticket with the log source details
options.D: Mute the payroll server's alerts until the maintenance ends

questions.key_concept: A log source that goes silent may signal compromise; follow the runbook's step even when an owner suggests a harmless cause.
questions.pre_read: Ask who the runbook gives this step to, and what would have to exist to explain the silence.
questions.correct_explanation: Attackers often stop logging to hide what they do, so the runbook treats an hour of silence from a log source as an incident to open. No change record covers the gap, and an owner's word is not one, so the maintenance theory is checked inside the ticket. Holding the ticket for the owner is the runner-up: owners know their systems, but an unrecorded explanation does not override the runbook.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the owner may be right. But no change record backs the claim, and the runbook already gives the ticket to the analyst; waiting gives any intruder more time.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a stuck agent is a common cause. But restarting it can change evidence, and closing the alert skips the investigation the runbook requires.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because maintenance alerts are noise. But muting a silent payroll server removes exactly the warning an attacker who stopped the logs would want gone.

tips: Eliminate: B restarts the agent and closes the alert, and D mutes the alerts; both treat a silent log as noise, not a warning sign.
Final two: C beats A because the runbook gives the ticket to the analyst and no change record backs the maintenance claim; that theory is checked inside the ticket, not before it.
Exam cue: a log source that goes quiet is itself an alert. Take the runbook's step, and test any harmless explanation inside the ticket.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-5 (Response to Audit Logging Process Failures); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a log source that goes silent is a possible sign of compromise and is handled as the runbook says' (notes 5.2.2 Logging and Monitoring). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A startup's security analyst sees an engineer who resigned yesterday downloading the whole design library at midnight; management and human resources decide any action on staff, including their access. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the engineer directly why they need the whole library
options.B: Disable the engineer's account to stop the downloads now
options.C: Warn the engineer's teammates to stop sharing files with them
options.D: Report it to the security manager with the download records

questions.key_concept: Suspected insider activity is reported discreetly, with evidence, to the security manager; management and human resources decide actions on staff.
questions.pre_read: Ask who in the stem may act on an employee, and what tipping off the person could cost.
questions.correct_explanation: A departing engineer copying the whole design library at midnight is a classic insider warning sign, and the analyst's job is to report it, with the download records, to the security manager without alerting anyone else. Disabling the account is the runner-up: it would stop the copying, but management and human resources decide actions on staff, including their access, so the analyst escalates rather than acting alone.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because asking seems fair and quick. But it tips off the engineer, who can delete traces or hurry the copying, and it oversteps the analyst's role.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it would stop the downloads. But actions on staff, including their access, are management's and human resources' decision here, so the analyst reports and lets them act.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because coworkers could help watch. But spreading a suspicion can harm someone innocent and may alert the engineer before the facts are known.

tips: Eliminate: A questions the engineer directly, and C tells coworkers; both can tip off a possible insider and spread an unproven suspicion.
Final two: D beats B because management and human resources decide actions on staff, including their access; the analyst reports with evidence instead of acting alone.
Exam cue: suspect an insider? Report it quietly to the security manager, with evidence. Never confront the person or tell coworkers.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(2) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Insider Threat); NIST CSF 2.0 DE.CM-03 (personnel activity and technology usage are monitored to find potentially adverse events)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'suspected insider activity is reported quietly with evidence, and management decides actions on staff' (notes 5.2.5 Threat Actors and Motives). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: Overnight, malicious code spreads across a shipyard's network from computer to computer through an unpatched file-sharing flaw, though no one opened any file. Which malware type should the system administrator report it as MOST accurately?

options.A: A computer virus
options.B: A Trojan horse
options.C: A rootkit
options.D: A computer worm

questions.key_concept: A worm spreads by itself across networks, often through unpatched flaws; a virus needs a host file that someone runs.
questions.pre_read: Notice how the code moved between computers, and whether any person had to do anything.
questions.correct_explanation: Malware that copies itself from computer to computer through a network flaw, with no one opening a file, is a worm; that self-spreading is why worms race through unpatched networks. A virus is the runner-up: it also spreads, but it rides inside a host file or program and usually needs someone to open or run it, and here nobody opened anything.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: viruses also spread across networks. But a virus rides in a host file that someone opens or runs; this code spread with no user action.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Trojans are common. But a Trojan relies on a user installing software that looks useful, and it does not copy itself to other computers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because hidden malware sounds serious. But a rootkit conceals activity on one system; it does not spread itself across a network.

tips: Eliminate: B needs a user to install it, and C conceals activity on one system; neither copies itself across a network.
Final two: D beats A because a worm spreads by itself through a flaw, while a virus needs a host file that someone runs.
Exam cue: spreads across the network with no user action? Worm. Needs a host file someone opens? Virus. Poses as useful software? Trojan horse.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1 Section 2.1 (Forms of Malware: viruses, worms and Trojan horses); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-2 (Flaw Remediation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a worm spreads by itself through network flaws, while a virus needs a host file that someone runs' (notes 5.2.8 Malware Basics). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A tram operator's journey-planner website is knocked offline by floods of requests from tens of thousands of hijacked devices whose addresses keep changing. Which control should the network team propose as BEST?

options.A: Block each flooding address on the website's own firewall
options.B: Require encrypted connections for every planner request
options.C: Have the internet provider filter the flood before it arrives
options.D: Reset the administrator passwords on the website's servers

questions.key_concept: A distributed denial-of-service attack is best filtered upstream, by the internet or hosting provider, before the flood reaches the organization's link.
questions.pre_read: Picture where the flood travels before it reaches the website, and how many senders there are.
questions.correct_explanation: Tens of thousands of hijacked devices with changing addresses make a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack, and the flood can fill the site's internet link before its own firewall even sees it. Filtering by the internet provider removes it upstream; NIST's incident guide suggests authorizing providers to contain large DDoS attacks. Blocking addresses is the runner-up: it works against one sender, not thousands that keep changing.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: blocking a source is a natural first step. But thousands of changing addresses outpace any block list, and the flood can fill the link before the firewall.
