wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption is a core control. But it protects confidentiality and integrity; an encrypted flood still overwhelms the site, so availability is not helped.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because an outage can look like a break-in. But a flood needs no access to the servers, so new passwords do nothing to stop it.

tips: Eliminate: B adds encryption, which protects confidentiality, not availability, and D resets passwords, though a flood needs no access to the servers.
Final two: C beats A because upstream filtering stops the flood before it fills the link; blocking one address at a time cannot keep up with thousands.
Exam cue: many changing sources means a distributed attack. Stop it upstream, at the provider, rather than one address at a time.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Table 3 (RS.MI-01: authorize internet and cloud service providers to contain certain incidents, such as large-scale DDoS attacks); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-5 (Denial-of-service Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a DDoS from many changing sources is filtered upstream by the provider, not address by address' (notes 5.2.9 Network Attacks: DoS, On-Path and Spoofing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A network technician at a business incubator sees a member's laptop answering address resolution protocol (ARP) requests for the gateway's IP address with the laptop's own hardware address. Which attack is MOST likely under way?

options.A: A denial-of-service attack flooding the gateway
options.B: An on-path attack routing other users' traffic through the laptop
options.C: An evil twin attack, with the laptop copying the incubator's Wi-Fi name
options.D: A replay attack resending sign-ins the laptop captured earlier

questions.key_concept: Forged ARP replies let a device on the local network pose as the gateway, which puts it on the path of other users' traffic.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the forged replies make other devices believe, and where their traffic will go next.
questions.correct_explanation: By answering ARP requests for the gateway's IP address with its own hardware address, the laptop tells other devices to send their gateway traffic to it, so it can read or change that traffic before passing it on: an on-path attack using ARP spoofing. An evil twin is the runner-up: it also puts the attacker on the path, but it works by broadcasting a fake Wi-Fi network, which nothing here shows.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the gateway is involved. But forged ARP replies redirect traffic rather than flood it; a denial-of-service attack aims to overload, not to intercept.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: an evil twin also puts the attacker in the path. But it needs a fake access point copying the network name; the evidence here is forged ARP replies.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because attackers do resend captured messages. But a replay reuses old sign-ins, while forged ARP replies redirect live traffic through the laptop.

tips: Eliminate: A describes flooding, which aims at availability, and D describes resending old messages; forged ARP replies do neither.
Final two: B beats C because forged ARP replies redirect traffic on the existing network; an evil twin needs a fake access point.
Exam cue: a device claiming another's address so traffic flows through it is spoofing used to get on-path. Name the attack by its goal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-23 (Session Authenticity); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-8(1) (Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity | Cryptographic Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'forged ARP replies put an attacker on the path between users and the gateway' (notes 5.2.9 Network Attacks: DoS, On-Path and Spoofing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A regional airport's firewall logs show packets arriving from the internet that carry source addresses from the airport's own internal network. Which control should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: Block inbound packets that bear internal source addresses
options.B: Log the packets and review them at the weekly firewall check
options.C: Block the real source addresses the packets were sent from
options.D: Add bandwidth so the packets do not slow the internal network

questions.key_concept: Source addresses are claims, not proof; an edge filter drops outside traffic that claims an internal source address.
questions.pre_read: Compare where these packets came from with the addresses they carry. Then ask what each option does about that mismatch.
questions.correct_explanation: Packets from the internet cannot genuinely come from internal addresses, so these addresses are spoofed, often to slip past rules that trust internal traffic. An edge filter that blocks inbound packets claiming internal sources stops the trick without knowing who sent them. Blocking the real senders is the runner-up: it sounds precise, but a spoofed header hides the true source, so there is no reliable address to block.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because logs build evidence. But a weekly review lets forged packets keep passing the firewall until then; an edge filter stops them now.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: stopping the real sender would end the attack. But a spoofed header hides the true source, so the firewall has no reliable address to block.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because extra packets can slow a network. But capacity answers a flood, not forged addresses; the spoofed packets would still get in.

tips: Eliminate: B only logs the forged packets for a later review, and D treats the problem as a flood; neither stops traffic that claims an internal address.
Final two: A beats C because a spoofed header hides the true sender; filtering on the impossible claim works without knowing who sent it.
Exam cue: treat addresses and sender names as claims. When outside traffic claims to be inside, drop it at the edge.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7(11) (Boundary Protection | Restrict Incoming Communications Traffic); NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2.1.1 (Packet Filtering: spoofed addresses in packet headers are used to get past firewall controls)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an edge filter drops outside traffic that claims an internal source address' (notes 5.2.9 Network Attacks: DoS, On-Path and Spoofing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: During a ransomware outbreak at a convention center, the electronic doors on a crowded hall's exit route fail locked. What should the on-site security analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Disconnect the door controllers from the network to stop the spread
options.B: Hold the exit doors open using each door's manual override
options.C: Photograph and log the exit door controllers' screens as evidence
options.D: Restore the door controllers from last night's backup copy

questions.key_concept: People's safety comes before containment, evidence and recovery: make people safe first, then the response continues.
questions.pre_read: Ask what is at stake for the people in the hall, and which steps can safely wait a few minutes.
questions.correct_explanation: People's safety outranks systems and evidence, so the first step is to release the locked exit doors with the manual override and keep the route open. Escape-route locks should fail safe with a manual release for exactly this case. Disconnecting the controllers is the runner-up: it is sound containment, but it does not free the doors, and containment can wait minutes while a trapped crowd cannot.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: containing ransomware matters. But disconnecting the controllers leaves the exits locked, and people's safety comes before stopping the spread.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because evidence helps the investigation. But a photograph can wait; while the exits stay locked, the crowd's safety comes first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because restoring would bring the doors back. But restoring before the infection is removed invites reinfection, and it is far slower than the manual override.

tips: Eliminate: C puts evidence ahead of a trapped crowd, and D restores devices before the ransomware is removed, inviting reinfection.
Final two: B beats A because people come first; containment matters, but it does not open the exits and can wait minutes.
Exam cue: when people are at risk, make them safe first. Containment, evidence and recovery follow.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 2.2.8 (Occupant Emergency Plan (OEP)); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'people's safety comes before containment, evidence and recovery during an incident' (notes 5.3.1 The Incident Response Plan and Team). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'/'with'; distractor C given 'and'.

questions.question: A bus company paused its fare-fraud model over suspected data poisoning, and its incident plan names the security analyst as evidence collector; the model's owner wants it retrained tonight. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Let the model owner's retraining go ahead, then collect the evidence
options.B: Save hashed copies of the current model and its training data
options.C: Delete the training records that look poisoned, then retrain
options.D: Search the live training data directly for poisoned records

questions.key_concept: Before an AI model is retrained or cleaned, preserve verified copies of the model and its training data as incident evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the incident plan gives the analyst, and how each option affects the model as it stands now.
questions.correct_explanation: The incident plan makes the analyst its evidence collector, so the first step is verified, hashed copies of the current model and its training data; retraining replaces the model and may overwrite the very records investigators need. Letting the owner retrain first is the runner-up: owners decide how their model is used, but the plan gives evidence collection to the analyst, and collecting afterward comes too late.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the owner does decide on retraining. But the plan makes the analyst its evidence collector, and evidence collected after retraining may already be overwritten.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because removing bad records sounds like a fix. But deleting suspected records destroys the evidence of what happened and how.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because finding the poisoned records is the goal. But analysis comes after preservation; investigators examine verified copies, so the originals stay exactly as found.

tips: Eliminate: C deletes the suspected records, and D works on the originals before copies are saved; both put the evidence the investigation needs at risk.
Final two: B beats A because the plan makes the analyst its evidence collector; once the owner retrains, the evidence may be gone.
Exam cue: before a model is retrained, rolled back or cleaned, save hashed copies of the model and its data. Fixes that overwrite evidence come second.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-07 (incident data and metadata are collected, and their integrity and provenance are preserved); NIST AI 100-2 E2025 (Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'preserve first, analyze later, and only within your role; investigators work on verified copies' (notes 5.3.4 Evidence Handling and Chain of Custody). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A car rental firm classifies customers' driver's license scans as restricted, its highest level, and an analyst's draft incident report includes screenshots of several. Which classification is MOST appropriate for the report?

options.A: Internal, since only named responders can see the restricted scans
options.B: Restricted, since the scans inside it set the report's level
options.C: Confidential, the level the incident report template sets
options.D: Unclassified, until the incident is closed and reviewed

questions.key_concept: Incident records take the classification of the most sensitive data they contain, whoever can open them today.
questions.pre_read: Ask what decides a document's classification: its contents, its template or who can see it.
questions.correct_explanation: A document takes the classification of the most sensitive data inside it, so a report holding restricted license scans is itself restricted and is handled that way wherever it goes. Internal is the runner-up: limiting it to named responders does narrow who sees it today, but access settings do not lower the classification, and the report may later be copied, printed or shared.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: only named responders can see it today. But who can see a document does not set its level; the restricted scans inside do.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because templates save effort. But a default label cannot lower the protection that the restricted scans inside the report require.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the report is still a draft. But drafts hold the same data, and leaving them unclassified invites careless sharing during the response.

tips: Eliminate: C lets a template default set the level, and D leaves a draft unclassified; content, not format or stage, sets classification.
Final two: B beats A because classification follows the most sensitive content; limiting who sees it does not lower its level.
Exam cue: a report inherits the highest classification of any data inside it, during an incident as at any other time.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Table 3 (RS.AN-06: incident response records can contain sensitive information and are safeguarded, with access for authorized personnel only); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.12 (Classification of information)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'incident records take the classification of the most sensitive data they contain' (notes 5.3.5 Data Handling During an Incident). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Key letter moved from C to B (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded to the same reason-clause form as A ('since', no 'data').

questions.question: An online furniture marketplace's incident plan relies on its cloud provider sending logs within an hour, which has never been tried. What should the incident response lead propose for the next tabletop as BEST?

options.A: Invite the provider's on-call contact to take part in the exercise
options.B: Ask the provider for a written promise to meet the one-hour target
options.C: Run the exercise on live systems so the provider's response is real
options.D: Leave the provider's part out and test only the internal roles

questions.key_concept: Exercises should include the third parties a plan depends on, so hand-offs such as log delivery are tested before a real incident.
questions.pre_read: Ask which part of the plan is untested, and who has to be in the room to test it.
questions.correct_explanation: The untested step is a hand-off to the cloud provider, so the provider's on-call contact should join the tabletop, where both sides walk through who asks, how, and how fast the logs arrive; gaps surface before a real incident. A written promise is the runner-up: it sets an expectation, but a signature does not show that the request route works or that anyone knows it.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a clear commitment helps. But a promise on paper does not test whether the request route works, who makes it, or how long it really takes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because live systems feel more realistic. But a tabletop is a discussion, and touching live systems risks real disruption for no extra learning here.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because internal roles are easier to arrange. But the provider's step is the untested part, so leaving it out tests everything except the gap.

tips: Eliminate: C runs a discussion exercise on live systems, risking disruption, and D leaves out the one untested step, the provider's hand-off.
Final two: A beats B because practicing the hand-off with the provider tests it; a written promise only states an expectation.
Exam cue: if the plan depends on an outside party, bring that party into the exercise. Untested hand-offs fail first in real incidents.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.IM-02 (improvements are identified from security tests and exercises, including those done in coordination with suppliers and relevant third parties); NIST SP 800-84 Section 4 (Tabletop Exercises: discussion-based events)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'exercises include the third parties a plan depends on, so their hand-offs are tested' (notes 5.3.7 Incident Response Exercises and Tabletops). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A textile mill's inventory lists its defect-spotting AI model but not the labeled photos used to tune it, kept on a shared drive. What should the system administrator propose as BEST?

options.A: Inventory the photo set separately, with an owner to classify it
options.B: Restrict the shared drive and list the photos under the model's entry
options.C: Delete the photo set, since tuning is finished
options.D: Move the photo set onto the model's server, already in the inventory

questions.key_concept: Training data is an AI asset in its own right, needing its own inventory entry, owner and classification, not just a note under the model.
questions.pre_read: Ask what could happen to the photos on the shared drive today, and what each option changes about that.
questions.correct_explanation: Anyone who can change or copy training data can poison or leak what the model learns, so the photo set needs its own inventory entry and an owner, who sets its classification; that level then decides who may change the photos and how they are protected. Restricting the drive is the runner-up: it is a useful control, but without an owner and classification nobody has decided what protection the photos need.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: locking the drive cuts exposure now. But without its own entry, owner and classification, nobody has decided what protection the photos need, so the lock is a guess.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because tuning is done. But the photos are needed to retrain or investigate the model, and deleting an asset is the owner's decision, not the administrator's.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because one entry seems tidy. But moving files gives the data no owner or classification, and the server's entry describes hardware, not data.

tips: Eliminate: C deletes data the model may need again, and D moves files without giving them an owner; neither brings the photos under management.
Final two: A beats B because ownership and classification decide what protection the photos need; locking the drive first only guesses at it.
Exam cue: training data shapes what a model learns, so it is an asset in its own right. Give it its own owner and classification, not a footnote under the model.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.6 (mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'training data is an AI asset of its own and needs its own inventory entry, owner and classification' (notes 5.4.1 Asset Inventory and Ownership). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: role IT asset analyst -> system administrator.

questions.question: A software vendor publishes four end dates for the ticketing system a planetarium runs. Which date should the system administrator flag as MOST important for protecting the system?

options.A: The end of sale, when new licenses can no longer be bought
options.B: The end of feature updates, when new functions and security features stop
options.C: The end of security patches, when fixes for new flaws stop
options.D: The end of the help line, when support calls stop being taken

questions.key_concept: For security, the end-of-life date that matters is when security patches stop; after it, newly found flaws stay open.
questions.pre_read: For each date, ask what stops arriving, and whether that thing protects the system from new flaws.
questions.correct_explanation: Once security patches stop, every newly found flaw stays open for good, so that date sets the deadline to replace the system or add compensating controls. The help line's end is the runner-up: vendors often call it the end of support, but losing phone help leaves no new flaw unfixed while security patches continue.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because end of sale signals the product's decline. But installed copies keep getting patches after sales stop, so security is not yet affected.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it mentions security features. But new security features are added functions; fixes for newly found flaws can continue after features stop, so this date matters less.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: vendors often call this the end of support. But losing phone help leaves no new flaw unfixed while security patches continue.

tips: Eliminate: A tracks new sales, and B tracks new functions, security features included; neither decides whether newly found flaws in the installed system get fixed.
Final two: C beats D because security depends on fixes for new flaws; the help line can end while patches continue.
Exam cue: for end-of-life questions, find the date security patches stop. That is the deadline to replace, isolate or add controls.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-22 (Unsupported System Components); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-02 (software is maintained, replaced, and removed commensurate with risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'for security, the end-of-life date that matters is when the vendor stops issuing security patches' (notes 5.4.3 End-of-Life Software and Devices). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A school district's patch tool reports that this month's browser fix installed on all 200 staff laptops. Which evidence BEST confirms to the system administrator that the browser flaw is closed?

options.A: A fresh vulnerability scan showing no laptop is still exposed
options.B: The patch tool's report of a successful install on each laptop
options.C: The approved change record for this month's patch rollout
options.D: Replies from users confirming they restarted their browsers

questions.key_concept: A patch is verified when an independent check, such as a rescan, shows the flaw is gone, not just when the installer reports success.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask what it actually measures: the rollout, its approval, the users or the laptops themselves.
questions.correct_explanation: Verification means checking that the patch took effect, not just that it ran. A fresh vulnerability scan tests each laptop for the flaw itself, catching machines where the install failed silently or never arrived. The patch tool's report is the runner-up: it shows the installer ran, but a reported install can still leave the flaw open, so it needs independent confirmation.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: install reports are useful records. But they show the installer ran, not that the flaw is gone; pending restarts or silent failures leave it open.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the change was properly approved. But approval shows the rollout was authorized, not that it worked on every laptop.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a restart often completes a browser patch. But user replies are incomplete and unreliable, and a restart alone does not prove the flaw is closed.

tips: Eliminate: C proves approval, not outcome, and D relies on user replies; neither shows the flaw is gone.
Final two: A beats B because a rescan tests for the flaw itself; an install report only shows the installer ran.
Exam cue: verify a fix by testing for the problem again. A rescan beats a success message from the tool that did the work.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4 Section 2.3.3 (Verify Deployment: confirm each patch installed successfully and took effect); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-5 (Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a patch is confirmed by an independent rescan that no longer finds the flaw' (notes 5.4.5 Patch Management). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A security operations team wants testers to run attacker techniques one at a time while its analysts check each for detection and tune rules on the spot. Which approach BEST fits this goal?

options.A: A red team engagement against the monitored network
options.B: A purple team exercise against the monitored network
options.C: A monthly vulnerability scan of the monitored servers
options.D: A tabletop exercise on a ransomware attack scenario

questions.key_concept: Purple teaming is red and blue working together in real time, so each attack step is checked for detection and gaps are fixed at once.
questions.pre_read: Ask which approach lets defenders check each attacker technique for detection while the test is still running.
questions.correct_explanation: In a purple team exercise, testers share each technique as they run it, so analysts can confirm whether it was detected and tune rules immediately; that is the step-by-step loop described. A red team engagement is the runner-up: it uses the same attacker techniques, but defenders usually learn what happened only from the final report, so tuning waits until the end.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: red teams run realistic attacker techniques. But defenders usually see the results only at the end, not step by step while tuning.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because scans test systems regularly. But a scan lists known weaknesses; it runs no attacker techniques and checks no detections.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tabletops are a team exercise. But they are discussions; nothing is run, so no detection can be checked or tuned.

tips: Eliminate: C lists weaknesses without attacking, and D only discusses a scenario; neither runs techniques against the detections.
Final two: B beats A because purple teaming shares each step in real time; a red team usually reports only at the end.
Exam cue: red attacks, blue defends, and purple is the two working together, sharing step by step to improve detection.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-8(2) (Penetration Testing | Red Team Exercises); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.IM-02 (improvements are identified from security tests and exercises, including those done in coordination with suppliers and relevant third parties)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'purple teaming is red and blue sharing each step in real time to improve detection' (notes 5.5.1 Red, Blue and Purple Teams). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A web team's app bundles 300 open-source libraries, and the team lead wants to know whether any have publicly known flaws. Which testing approach BEST fits this need?

options.A: Static analysis of the team's own source code
options.B: Penetration testing of the deployed app by an outside firm
options.C: Fuzz testing of the app's input handling with random data
options.D: Software composition analysis of the app's components

questions.key_concept: Software composition analysis lists the third-party components an app uses and flags versions with publicly known flaws.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose code is in question, the team's own or someone else's, and what kind of flaw is sought.
questions.correct_explanation: Software composition analysis inventories the libraries an app bundles and checks each version against databases of publicly known flaws, which is exactly the question asked. Static analysis is the runner-up: it also examines code without running it, but it looks for coding mistakes in the team's own source and does not match library versions to published flaws.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: static analysis also examines code early. But it hunts coding mistakes in the team's own code; it does not match library versions to published flaws.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because penetration tests find real weaknesses. But testers probe the running app from outside; they do not inventory every bundled library and match its version to published flaws.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fuzzing finds crashes and input flaws. But it feeds random data to the app; it does not list the bundled libraries or check them against published flaws.

tips: Eliminate: B probes the deployed app from outside, and C feeds it random input; neither lists the bundled library versions.
Final two: D beats A because composition analysis matches each library version to known flaws; static analysis looks for mistakes in the team's own code.
Exam cue: someone else's code with publicly known flaws? Software composition analysis. Your own code, before it runs? SAST.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF v1.1) PW.4.4 (verify third-party software components, including automatic detection of known vulnerabilities); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-11(1) (Developer Testing and Evaluation | Static Code Analysis)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'software composition analysis checks bundled third-party components for publicly known flaws' (notes 5.5.3 Static and Dynamic Application Testing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 5.5 Security testing. Threat modeling AI features
questions.question: Threat modeling a park service's planned AI chatbot that reads public web pages to answer visitors, a security analyst examines where those pages enter the model. Which threat is MOST relevant at that point?

options.A: Hidden page instructions that steer what the chatbot tells visitors
options.B: Poisoned web pages slipped into the vendor's original training data
options.C: Visitors sharing their sign-in passwords with one another
options.D: Theft of the server that hosts the chatbot's software

questions.key_concept: Where outside content enters an AI model is a trust boundary: hidden instructions in that content can steer the model, called indirect prompt injection.
questions.pre_read: Ask what crosses into the model at that point, who controls it, and what it could make the model do.
questions.correct_explanation: Public web pages are untrusted input crossing into the model, and because models mix data and instructions, text hidden in a page can steer the chatbot's answers: indirect prompt injection. That is the threat at this boundary. Poisoned training data is the runner-up: it is a real AI threat, but it enters during the vendor's training, not where live pages reach the model.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: poisoning is a real AI threat. But it enters during the vendor's training, not at this boundary, where live pages reach the model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because shared passwords are a common weakness. But that threat sits at sign-in, not where web pages enter the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because physical theft is a real risk. But it belongs to the hosting site, not to the flow where pages reach the model.

tips: Eliminate: C is a sign-in issue, and D a physical one; neither happens where web pages flow into the model.
Final two: A beats B because pages entering at run time can carry hidden instructions; poisoning happens earlier, during the vendor's training.
Exam cue: at each trust boundary, ask what untrusted input crosses and what it could make the system do. For AI, that includes hidden instructions.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 3.4 (Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks and Mitigations: attackers plant instructions in resources the model reads); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-11(2) (Developer Testing and Evaluation | Threat Modeling and Vulnerability Analyses)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'where outside content enters an AI model is a trust boundary where hidden instructions can steer it' (notes 5.5.4 Threat Modeling). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: role junior analyst -> security analyst.

questions.question: At a satellite operator's ground station, a night guard finds someone in the equipment room who shows a signed letter naming them as an authorized penetration tester. What should the guard do FIRST?

options.A: Let them continue with the test that the letter describes
options.B: Phone the letter's signer on the number printed on that letter
options.C: Keep them in sight and call the security team's known contact
options.D: Send them off site and record the visit in the shift log

questions.key_concept: Physical tests are pre-arranged with the security team, so guards confirm a claimed tester through its known contact; a letter is a claim, not proof.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the guard has been handed and what it can prove. Then ask how each option would check it.
questions.correct_explanation: A letter is only a claim: an intruder could forge one and print an accomplice's number on it. A real test is arranged with the security team in advance, so the guard keeps the person in view and calls that team's known contact. Calling the number printed on the letter is the runner-up: it looks like verification, but the letter came from the visitor, so its number may reach an accomplice.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the letter is signed and looks official. But signatures can be forged, and letting someone continue unverified is what a real intruder hopes for.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it does try to verify the claim. But a forged letter can print an accomplice's number, so the check runs through details the visitor controls.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because removing them seems safe. But a real intruder simply walks away unverified, leaving only a log entry, and a genuine test is cut short without a check.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts the letter at face value, and D lets a possible intruder leave unverified; both skip confirming who the person is.
Final two: C beats B because the guard already knows the security team's contact; a number printed on the visitor's own letter could reach an accomplice.
Exam cue: a claimed tester counts as an intruder until the team that arranged the test confirms them. Letters and numbers the visitor brings prove nothing on their own.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-115 Section 5.2 (Penetration Testing: security guards should be made aware of how to verify the validity of tester activity); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-3 (Physical Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'verify a claimed tester through a known contact, never through details the visitor supplies' (notes 5.5.5 Physical and Social Engineering Penetration Tests). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A documentary studio's AI tool labels a client's merger contract Internal, but its deal terms fit the policy's Confidential level, and data owners set levels. What should the security analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Protect it as Confidential pending the owner's decision
options.B: Relabel it Confidential and record the change in a ticket
options.C: Keep the Internal label unless the data owner raises a concern
options.D: Report the wrong label to the vendor for retraining

questions.key_concept: AI labeling tools only suggest a level; the data owner decides, and data that looks mislabeled is protected at the higher level meanwhile.
questions.pre_read: Ask who has the authority to set a classification level.
questions.correct_explanation: Automatic labels, including AI ones, are only suggestions; the data owner's decision governs. When a label looks too low, the analyst protects the data at the higher level and sends the label back to its owner. Relabeling it Confidential is the runner-up: the new level is probably right, but setting it is the owner's call, and recording it in a ticket does not make it the analyst's.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the new level is likely right and the change is recorded. But setting a classification is the data owner's decision, not the analyst's, however clear it looks.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the tool labels files routinely. But an AI label is only a suggestion, and leaving deal terms at Internal underprotects them while waiting.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fixing the tool could prevent repeats. But it leaves this contract underprotected now, and the vendor cannot decide the contract's level either.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts an AI label the content contradicts, and D fixes future labels while this contract stays underprotected; neither settles this file's level.
Final two: A beats B because the data owner sets the level; the analyst protects the file at the higher level meanwhile instead of deciding it.
Exam cue: when a label looks wrong, protect at the higher level and ask the owner. AI labeling tools suggest; owners decide.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-16 (Security and Privacy Attributes); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Information Owner/Steward)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'automatic labels only suggest; the data owner decides, and the data is protected at the higher level meanwhile' (notes 5.1.1 Data Classification and Labeling). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'/'data'/'owner'; distractor D without 'so'/'is'.

questions.subtopic: 5.1 Data security. Sharing with third parties
questions.question: A chamber choir will send its Confidential donor list to a mailing house for a three-month campaign. What should the security analyst propose as BEST to protect the list while the mailing house holds it?

options.A: Label the file Confidential so the mailing house handles it with care
options.B: Accept the mailing house's privacy policy as its safeguard
options.C: Encrypt the list for transfer and send its password by another route
options.D: Write handling rules and deletion into the mailing contract

questions.key_concept: Handling rules follow data across its lifecycle; when a third party receives it, a contract carries those rules, including deletion after use.
questions.pre_read: Recall what handling rules cover and who has to follow them.
questions.correct_explanation: Handling rules follow the label at every stage, including when data goes to a third party. A contract makes the mailing house follow the choir's rules for a Confidential list and delete it when the campaign ends. Encrypting the transfer is the runner-up: it is good practice, but it protects the list only on the way; once decrypted, nothing governs how it is stored, used or destroyed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because labels tell people how sensitive data is. But a label places no duty on an outside company to store, limit or delete the list.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor promises to protect personal data. But its policy is its own, can change, and does not commit it to the choir's rules or to deletion.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: encrypting the transfer with a separate password is sound. But it protects the list only in transit; after decryption, nothing sets how it is kept or destroyed.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a label that binds no outsider, and B relies on the vendor's own policy; neither makes the choir's rules apply at the mailing house.
Final two: D beats C because encryption covers only the transfer; a contract carries the handling rules, including deletion, to where the data is used.
Exam cue: when sensitive data goes to a third party, its handling rules travel by contract. Protecting the transfer alone leaves the rest of the lifecycle open.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-05 (requirements to address cybersecurity risks in supply chains are established, prioritized and integrated into contracts and other agreements with suppliers); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-9 (External System Services)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'handling rules travel with data to a third party by contract, including deletion after use' (notes 5.1.2 Data Handling Across the Lifecycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A cooking school's 12 instructors must each be able to message every other instructor privately, using symmetric encryption only. Which key count is MOST accurate for the IT technician to plan for?

options.A: 12 keys, one secret key held by each instructor
options.B: 24 keys, a public and a private key for each instructor
options.C: 66 keys, one secret key for each pair of instructors
options.D: 132 keys, one secret key for each direction between two instructors

questions.key_concept: Symmetric encryption needs one shared key per pair of people, n(n−1)/2; asymmetric encryption needs one key pair per person, 2n.
questions.pre_read: Work out who must share a secret with whom, then count.
questions.correct_explanation: With symmetric encryption, each pair of people who message privately shares its own secret key. Twelve instructors form 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66 pairs, so 66 keys. Twenty-four is the runner-up: it is the count for asymmetric encryption, where each person holds one key pair (2n), which is why asymmetric methods scale better as groups grow.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because one key each sounds tidy. But everyone sending to an instructor would need that same key, so every holder could read the others' messages.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: 24 is a real key count, for asymmetric encryption with one key pair per person. The stem allows symmetric only, which needs one shared key per pair.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because messages flow both ways. But one shared symmetric key works in both directions, so counting each direction separately doubles the true total.

tips: Eliminate: A gives each instructor one key that every sender would have to share, and D double-counts, since one shared key covers both directions.
Final two: C beats B because 24 is the asymmetric count, 2n; symmetric needs one key per pair, n(n−1)/2, which for 12 people is 66.
Exam cue: symmetric keys grow with pairs, n(n−1)/2; asymmetric keys grow with people, 2n. Check which kind the stem allows before counting.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.1 (Data Encryption); NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 (Recommendation for Key Management: Part 1 – General)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'symmetric encryption needs one shared key per pair, n(n-1)/2; asymmetric needs one key pair per person' (notes 5.1.5 Symmetric and Asymmetric Encryption). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: Before restoring a building society's ledger backup, the system administrator finds its SHA-256 hash matches the value stored in a protected log when it was written. What does the match MOST accurately show?

options.A: Only authorized staff have opened the backup since it was written
options.B: The backup has not changed since it was written
options.C: An authorized administrator created the backup and its record
options.D: The backup holds no malware and is safe to restore now

questions.key_concept: A matching hash from a trusted record shows data is unchanged, not who made it, who read it or whether it is clean.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a plain hash takes as input, and what it can and cannot prove.
questions.correct_explanation: A hash is a fixed-length fingerprint: change one bit and it changes completely. A match against a value kept somewhere trusted shows the backup is unchanged since that value was recorded. Safe to restore is the runner-up: an unchanged backup feels clean, but malware saved into it before it was hashed matches its own hash perfectly.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the log was protected. But a hash hides nothing and records no access; it says the data is unchanged, not who has read it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the stored value was protected. But a plain hash uses no secret, so anyone could compute one; showing who made the backup needs an HMAC or a signature.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a match rules out tampering since the backup was written. But malware saved into it before then matches its own hash, so it still needs scanning.

tips: Eliminate: A treats hashing as an access record, and C treats it as proof of who made the backup, which a plain hash with no key cannot give.
Final two: B beats D because a hash shows only that the backup is unchanged; malware saved into it before hashing matches perfectly, so scan before restoring.
Exam cue: a matching hash proves integrity, not cleanliness. Before restoring, also check the backup predates the compromise and scan it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.2 (Integrity); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.3.1 (Secret Key Electronic Signatures)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a matching hash shows integrity only, not origin, secrecy or cleanliness' (notes 5.1.6 Hashing, Digital Signatures and Certificates). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 5.1 Data security. Buying for quantum risk
questions.question: A mortgage lender is buying a VPN appliance to run for ten years, carrying loan files that must stay secret for decades. Which requirement should the security analyst propose as BEST for quantum risk?

options.A: AES-256 for tunnel traffic in place of today's AES-128
options.B: Post-quantum key exchange, via a vendor upgrade if not built in
options.C: RSA key exchange with 8,192-bit keys in place of 2,048-bit ones
options.D: No quantum requirement until a working quantum computer exists

questions.key_concept: Quantum risk falls on public-key key exchange and signatures; long-lived systems guarding long-lived secrets need post-quantum support or an upgrade path.
questions.pre_read: Notice how long the appliance will run and how long the files must stay secret. Then weigh each option.
questions.correct_explanation: A quantum computer threatens the public-key methods VPNs use to agree session keys, and traffic recorded today could be decrypted later, while these files must stay secret for decades. So the appliance needs post-quantum key exchange, such as NIST's ML-KEM, or a firm upgrade path. Longer RSA keys are the runner-up: more bits usually add strength, but a quantum computer breaks RSA at any size, and NIST disallows quantum-vulnerable key exchange after 2035.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AES-256 does resist quantum attacks. But bulk encryption was not the weak point; the session keys are still agreed with public-key methods a quantum computer could break.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: longer keys usually add strength. But quantum attacks break RSA's math at any key size, and NIST disallows quantum-vulnerable key exchange after 2035, within this appliance's ten years.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because no such computer exists yet. But traffic recorded today can be decrypted later, and these files must stay secret for decades.

tips: Eliminate: A strengthens bulk encryption, which was never the weak point, and D waits, though traffic recorded now can be decrypted later.
Final two: B beats C because quantum attacks break RSA whatever its key size, and NIST disallows quantum-vulnerable key exchange after 2035, inside this appliance's ten years.
Exam cue: longer RSA keys are no quantum fix. Replace public-key key exchange, and for long-lived purchases require post-quantum support or a firm upgrade path.
questions.framework_ref: NIST FIPS 203 Section 1.2 (Context: large-scale quantum computers would put public-key key establishment and signatures at risk); NIST IR 8547 Section 4.1.2 (Key Establishment: quantum-vulnerable key-establishment schemes, including RSA, are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'long-lived systems protecting long-lived secrets need post-quantum key exchange or an upgrade path' (notes 5.1.7 Quantum-Resistant Cryptography). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'or'.

questions.subtopic: 5.2 Security operations. Several alerts at once
questions.question: Within ten minutes, a robotics startup's monitoring tool shows a phishing-link click, an endpoint malware alert and a new sign-in from abroad, all for one engineer. What should the security analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Work the three alerts one at a time in arrival order
options.B: Close the click alert, since the email filter logged it
options.C: Escalate the three alerts together as one linked case
options.D: Escalate only the sign-in alert, the highest rated of the three

questions.key_concept: Correlation joins related alerts for the same user or host into one case, revealing an attack chain that single alerts hide.
questions.pre_read: Read all three alerts together before deciding what any one of them means.
questions.correct_explanation: Correlation links related events for the same user and time into one case. A click, a malware alert and an unusual sign-in within minutes tell one story: phishing led to compromise. The analyst escalates that whole case. Escalating only the sign-in is the runner-up: it is the highest single alert, but alone it hides how the attacker got in and which device to contain.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because working in order seems fair and thorough. But it splits one attack into three tickets and can leave the riskiest part waiting.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the filter recorded the email. But the click starts the chain; the malware and sign-in that followed show it was not harmless.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the sign-in is the most serious alert alone. But escalating it by itself hides the phishing click and infected device that responders must also contain.

tips: Eliminate: A handles linked alerts separately by arrival, and B closes the click that the other two alerts show was the way in.
Final two: C beats D because correlated alerts tell one attack story; escalating the sign-in alone leaves out the email and the infected endpoint.
Exam cue: same user, short window, several alert types? Correlate them into one case before ranking, then escalate the whole case.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 DE.AE-03 (information is correlated from multiple sources); NIST CSF 2.0 RS.MA-04 (incidents are escalated or elevated as needed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'correlate related alerts for one user and time window into one case before ranking and escalating' (notes 5.2.3 Event Triage: Use Cases, Prioritization and Correlation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'.

questions.question: A go-kart track's security analyst reads a two-year-old intelligence report on a ransomware group that still targets leisure businesses. Which part of the report is MOST likely to still be useful?

options.A: Its description of the methods the group uses to get in
options.B: Its list of the IP addresses the group attacked from
options.C: Its list of the domains and email senders in the group's phishing
options.D: Its hash values for the group's ransomware program files

questions.key_concept: Technical indicators go stale quickly as attackers change infrastructure and files; descriptions of attacker methods stay useful much longer.
questions.pre_read: Notice the report's age, then consider each part of it in turn.
questions.correct_explanation: Indicators such as addresses, domains and file hashes are cheap for attackers to change, so they go stale fast. A group's methods, how it gets in, moves and spreads, take effort to change and stay useful for detection and defense far longer. File hashes are the runner-up: they identify exact files, but any small rebuild of the ransomware gives it a new hash.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because blocking attack sources sounds direct. But attackers switch addresses often, and two-year-old ones may now belong to innocent users.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because blocking phishing domains works on fresh reports. But such domains and senders are cheap and short-lived, and many will have expired or changed owners.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: hashes pinpoint known malicious files. But changing a single byte gives a new hash, so two-year-old values miss every rebuilt version.

tips: Eliminate: B and C are infrastructure, addresses and domains, which attackers rotate cheaply, so old values are stale and may now block innocent sites.
Final two: A beats D because a tiny rebuild changes a file's hash, while the group's way of getting in and spreading is costly to change.
Exam cue: indicators of compromise age fast; knowledge of attacker behavior ages slowly. Use old reports for methods and fresh feeds for indicators.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-150 Section 2.1 (Threat Information Types: indicators are technical artifacts, while TTPs describe an actor's behavior); NIST SP 800-150 Section 4.4 (Organize and Store Cyber Threat Information: record how long each indicator is still considered valid)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'indicators go stale quickly while knowledge of attacker methods stays useful longer' (notes 5.2.6 Cyber Threat Intelligence). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'how'/'and'; distractor C given 'and'.

questions.question: An aviary's security manager asks the analyst to use MITRE ATT&CK to plan next year's detection work for a small team. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Build one new detection for every technique in the matrix
options.B: Map current detections to the techniques seen at similar organizations
options.C: Adopt ATT&CK as the aviary's required set of security controls
options.D: Report progress as the share of all matrix techniques the team detects

questions.key_concept: MITRE ATT&CK is used selectively: map current detections against the techniques likely attackers use, then close the most relevant gaps.
questions.pre_read: Recall what kind of resource ATT&CK is and how large it is.
questions.correct_explanation: ATT&CK is a map of real attacker behavior, not a checklist. Mapping existing detections against the techniques seen at similar organizations shows the gaps that matter most, so a small team spends its effort where attacks are likely. Building a detection for every technique is the runner-up: it sounds thorough, but the matrix holds hundreds of techniques, many irrelevant to the aviary.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: wider coverage sounds safer. But the matrix holds hundreds of techniques, and a small team chasing all of them neglects the ones likely attackers use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because ATT&CK is widely respected. But it is a knowledge base of attacker behavior, not a standard of required controls.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a coverage figure is easy to report. But it rewards covering easy techniques over likely ones and says little about real risk.

tips: Eliminate: C turns a knowledge base into a control standard, and D measures matrix coverage instead of protection against likely attackers.
Final two: B beats A because ATT&CK is a map, not a checklist; covering the techniques likely attackers use beats spreading a small team across all of them.
Exam cue: use ATT&CK selectively: map what you detect, compare it with what likely attackers do, and close those gaps first.
questions.framework_ref: MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base (Enterprise matrix: tactics and techniques); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-03 (internal and external threats to the organization are identified and recorded)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'ATT&CK is used selectively to find detection gaps against likely attackers' techniques' (notes 5.2.7 Threat Frameworks: MITRE ATT&CK and the Kill Chain). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key given 'the' (all distractors carried it).

questions.question: An attacker on a brickworks' network captured a supervisor's valid sign-in to the timesheet server and resent it later to get in, never learning the password. Which control should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: Encrypt the sign-in messages so no one can read them
options.B: Make each sign-in answer a fresh, one-time challenge
options.C: Require longer and more complex passwords for every staff member
options.D: Block the attacker's laptop by its media access control (MAC) address

questions.key_concept: A replay attack resends a captured valid message; fresh one-time challenges, called nonces, make old copies useless, which encryption alone does not.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the attacker did with the captured message, and what they never needed to know.
questions.correct_explanation: This is a replay attack: a captured, valid message is sent again. The attacker never read or changed it, so the defense is freshness. When the server issues a new one-time challenge, called a nonce, for each sign-in, an old copy no longer matches and fails. Encryption is the runner-up: it stops reading, but an encrypted message can be resent unread and still be accepted.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: encryption stops eavesdroppers reading the message. But the attacker only resent it; an encrypted copy replays just as well unless each sign-in is unique.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because stronger passwords resist guessing. But the attacker never needed the password; they reused a whole captured sign-in.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it targets the device that attacked. But hardware addresses are easily copied, and any other device could replay a capture.

tips: Eliminate: C strengthens a password the attacker never needed, and D trusts a hardware address that can be faked; neither stops an old message working again.
Final two: B beats A because a replayed message need not be read; encryption hides content, while a one-time challenge makes each sign-in unrepeatable.
Exam cue: a captured message resent later is a replay attack. The fix is freshness: nonces, timestamps or one-time challenges.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-2(8) (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users) | Access to Accounts — Replay Resistant); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-23 (Session Authenticity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a replayed message is defeated by freshness, such as one-time challenges, not by encryption alone' (notes 5.2.9 Network Attacks: DoS, On-Path and Spoofing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: During a data-extortion attack on an amusement pier, the attackers post a ride technician's home address online with a threat of violence. What should the incident response lead do FIRST?

options.A: Message the attackers to ask them to take the post down
options.B: Report the threat to the security manager and await direction
options.C: Log the threat to the technician and carry on with containment
options.D: Warn the technician, then arrange protection through human resources

questions.key_concept: An incident's harm can reach people off the network: when attackers threaten staff, warn them and bring in those who can protect them first.
questions.pre_read: Recall who leads an incident response and what they may decide without waiting.
questions.correct_explanation: Attackers' threats can reach people far from the network. A threat of violence against a named employee at home puts a person in danger, so the lead first warns the technician and arranges their safety with human resources, who can involve physical security or the police. Reporting to the security manager and waiting is the runner-up: management should know, but the lead already has authority to act, and waiting leaves the technician unwarned.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because removing the post would help the technician. But contacting attackers is for management and legal counsel to decide, and it can invite more pressure.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the security manager should hear of a threat this serious. But the lead can direct the response, and waiting leaves the technician unwarned and in danger.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because containment stops the ransomware spreading. But it treats a threat of violence as a log entry while a person may be in danger.

tips: Eliminate: A opens talks with attackers, which management and legal counsel decide, and C files the threat away while technical work continues.
Final two: D beats B because the lead directs the response and a person may be in danger now; the security manager can be told once the technician is warned and protection is being arranged.
Exam cue: threats against staff reach beyond the network. Warn the person and bring in those who can protect them, such as human resources or the police, before approvals, evidence or containment.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Table 2 (GV.RM-03: incident decisions are informed by other risks, such as safety, not just cybersecurity risks in isolation); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-8 (Incident Response Plan)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'when an incident puts a person in danger, making them safe comes before evidence and containment' (notes 5.3.1 The Incident Response Plan and Team). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'/'with'. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded as 'X, then Y', without the comma-ing tail.

questions.subtopic: 5.3 Incident response. Phases and CSF functions
questions.question: A tennis club's incident playbook lists two steps: isolate infected laptops and remove the malware from them. Under NIST CSF 2.0, which function do these steps MOST accurately fall under?

options.A: The Detect function
options.B: The Recover function
options.C: The Respond function
options.D: The Protect function

questions.key_concept: Under CSF 2.0, containment and eradication are Respond outcomes; Recover restores operations, and Detect finds and analyzes events.
questions.pre_read: Recall the six CSF 2.0 functions and what each one covers.
questions.correct_explanation: SP 800-61 Rev. 3 maps the classic phases onto CSF 2.0: preparation to Govern, Identify and Protect; detection and analysis to Detect; containment, eradication and recovery to Respond and Recover. Containing an incident and removing its cause are Respond outcomes. Recover is the runner-up: it shares that phase group, but it covers restoring systems and operations afterward.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because detection starts incident work. But Detect covers finding and analyzing possible attacks, not stopping or removing them.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Recover shares the old containment, eradication and recovery phase. But it covers restoring operations; containing and eradicating are Respond outcomes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because containment protects other systems. But Protect covers safeguards set up before incidents, such as access control and training.

tips: Eliminate: A covers finding and analyzing events, and D covers safeguards in place before any incident; neither covers acting on a confirmed one.
Final two: C beats B because CSF 2.0 lists containing and eradicating incidents under Respond, while Recover restores assets and operations afterward.
Exam cue: Govern, Identify and Protect prepare; Detect finds; Respond contains and eradicates; Recover restores. Improvement runs throughout.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Table 1 (Previous incident response life cycle model's phases and corresponding CSF 2.0 Functions); NIST CSF 2.0 RS.MI-01 (incidents are contained); NIST CSF 2.0 RS.MI-02 (incidents are eradicated)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'containment and eradication map to the CSF 2.0 Respond function' (notes 5.3.2 The Incident Response Lifecycle and CSF 2.0). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 5.3 Incident response. Evidence from a running server
questions.question: A yacht club's incident plan names the system administrator as evidence collector, and a compromised booking server, owned by the operations manager, is still running. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Capture the server's memory, then image its disk
options.B: Ask the operations manager, as owner, whether to collect evidence
options.C: Image the server's disk, then capture its memory
options.D: Leave the server untouched for trained forensic staff to collect

questions.key_concept: Staff the plan names as evidence collectors capture volatile data, such as memory, before disk contents; others preserve the scene and report.
questions.pre_read: Notice who the plan names for which task, and what is still running.
questions.correct_explanation: Evidence collection is the administrator's job here, because the plan names them; that is what lets them act rather than wait. Volatile data, such as memory and network connections, disappears at shutdown or over time, so it is captured before the disk, which persists. Leaving it for forensic staff is the runner-up: right for staff the plan does not name, but here it risks losing the memory evidence.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the server belongs to the operations manager. But the plan already assigns evidence collection; owners advise on recovery priorities, not on whether evidence is kept.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the disk holds most of the data. But disk contents survive shutdown while memory does not, so the more volatile memory comes first.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: leaving evidence to trained staff is right for anyone the plan does not name. Here the plan names the administrator, and waiting risks losing memory.

tips: Eliminate: B asks the owner for a decision the plan already made, and C copies the disk first, though memory is lost first.
Final two: A beats D because the plan names the administrator as collector; hands-off is the rule only for staff the plan does not name.
Exam cue: collect evidence only if the plan names you; if it does, take the most volatile data, such as memory, before the disk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-86 Section 3.1.2 (Acquiring the Data: acquiring volatile data should usually be given priority over non-volatile data); NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-07 (incident data and metadata are collected, and their integrity and provenance are preserved)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'staff the plan names as evidence collectors take the most volatile data first' (notes 5.3.4 Evidence Handling and Chain of Custody). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An audiobook publisher's latest account takeover had the same root cause as one last year, whose agreed fix is months overdue; management approves improvement work. What should the incident response lead do FIRST?

options.A: Raise the overdue fix with management as a repeat cause
options.B: Add the overdue fix to this review's list with a new date
options.C: Close last year's action, since this review covers the same cause
options.D: Make the fix personally, then report it to management

questions.key_concept: Lessons learned actions are tracked to completion; an overdue fix behind a repeat incident is raised with management, who approve and fund improvements.
questions.pre_read: Recall what happens to lessons learned actions after the review.
questions.correct_explanation: A repeat root cause shows last year's improvement never happened. Management approves improvement work, so the lead raises the overdue fix and the repeat with them, with the evidence, so it gets owned, resourced and done. Re-adding the fix with a new date is the runner-up: it keeps a record, but it repeats what already failed without anyone with authority seeing why it stalled.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a new due date keeps the fix on the list. But the same step already slipped once; without management seeing the repeat and the stall, nothing changes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because this review covers the same cause. But closing the old action hides that a promised fix was never made.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because doing it yourself seems fastest. But management approves improvement work, and quietly making the fix skips the question of why it stalled and who owns it.

tips: Eliminate: C closes an action whose fix was never made, and D has the lead take over a fix that management has to approve.
Final two: A beats B because the same fix already slipped once; management, who approve improvement work, must see the repeat cause to get it done.
Exam cue: lessons learned actions are tracked to completion. An overdue fix behind a repeat incident goes, with evidence, to whoever approves the work.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.IM-03 (improvements are identified from execution of operational processes, procedures, and activities)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an overdue lessons learned fix behind a repeat incident is raised with management, who approve and fund improvements' (notes 5.3.6 Lessons Learned and Continuous Improvement). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An eyewear retailer's inventory lists nine store laptops, owned by the store managers, that no scan has seen for months; procedure has the system administrator trace them. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Delete the nine laptops from the inventory as unused
options.B: Report all nine to the incident response lead as lost devices
options.C: Ask the store managers, as owners, to decide what happens next
options.D: Contact each laptop's assigned user to confirm where it is

questions.key_concept: Inventory gaps are investigated, not deleted; when procedure assigns tracing to the practitioner, they trace first and report what cannot be found.
questions.pre_read: Notice who owns the laptops and who the procedure gives the task to.
questions.correct_explanation: The procedure gives tracing to the administrator, so they act on it, even though store managers own the laptops. Contacting each assigned user quickly separates laptops that are simply unused or offline from ones truly missing. Reporting all nine as lost is the runner-up: any laptop that cannot be found should be reported, but declaring nine lost devices before checking skips the step the procedure sets.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because unseen laptops look retired. But deleting the records hides devices that may still exist and hold customer data, the opposite of what an inventory is for.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a laptop that cannot be found should be reported. But the procedure says trace first, and most unseen laptops are simply idle or offline.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the store managers own the laptops. But the procedure already gives tracing to the administrator; owners decide how laptops are used, not whether they are traced.

tips: Eliminate: A deletes records for devices that may still hold data, and C hands owners a task the procedure already gives the administrator.
Final two: D beats B because the procedure puts tracing first; laptops that still cannot be found are then reported as lost, with the facts.
Exam cue: an asset that drops out of scans is traced before its record changes. Remove a record only after disposal is confirmed, and report what cannot be found.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-01 (inventories of hardware managed by the organization are maintained); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-8 (System Component Inventory)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'inventory gaps are investigated, not deleted; when procedure assigns tracing, the practitioner traces first' (notes 5.4.1 Asset Inventory and Ownership). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: role IT asset analyst -> system administrator.

questions.question: An olive oil cooperative replaced its AI pricing model, and the asset owner approved retiring the old one, whose cloud endpoint still answers requests. What should the system administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Leave the endpoint running until the cloud contract ends
options.B: Keep the endpoint live as a fallback for the new model
options.C: Delete the old model's entry from the asset inventory
options.D: Shut down the old endpoint and revoke the keys that reach it

questions.key_concept: Retiring an AI model, like any asset, removes its access first, endpoints and keys, before records are closed and its data is disposed of.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the owner has already decided and what can still be reached.
questions.correct_explanation: Retirement removes an asset's access before its records are closed. The owner approved retiring the old model, so the administrator shuts its endpoint and revokes the keys that reach it, then updates the inventory and disposes of its data by procedure. Keeping it as a fallback is the runner-up: it sounds prudent, but that is a decision the owner did not make, and an idle endpoint drifts out of patching and monitoring.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the endpoint is already paid for. But a retired model left answering requests keeps a way in that nobody watches until the contract ends.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a fallback can be useful during a model change. But the owner approved retirement, and an unused endpoint left live drifts out of patching and monitoring.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because records should match reality. But deleting the entry first makes a still-running endpoint invisible to the people who patch and monitor assets.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves a retired endpoint open until a contract date, and C deletes its record while it still answers requests, so no one patches or watches it.
Final two: D beats B because the owner already approved retirement; keeping a fallback is a new decision, and an idle endpoint is an unwatched way in.
Exam cue: AI models follow the same lifecycle as other assets. At retirement, remove access first, then update records and dispose of data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.7 (processes and procedures are in place for decommissioning and phasing out AI systems safely); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-08 (systems, hardware, software, services, and data are managed throughout their life cycles)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'retiring an AI model removes its access first, then records are closed and data disposed of' (notes 5.4.2 The Asset Lifecycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: distractor B reworded without 'if'.

questions.question: A kombucha brewer's policy allows unsupported systems only by an exception the policy owner approves, and its fermentation-control PC must run unsupported another year. What is BEST for the security analyst to ensure is recorded?

options.A: A shift-log note saying the policy owner has approved the exception
options.B: A risk register entry in which the risk owner accepts the risk
options.C: A vendor review saying the unsupported PC is still safe to run
options.D: A time-limited, approved exception with conditions and a review

questions.key_concept: Keeping an unsupported system against policy needs a documented, time-limited exception with conditions and a review, not a risk acceptance alone.
questions.pre_read: Recall what keeping an unsupported system running requires.
questions.correct_explanation: This policy allows an unsupported system only by an exception the policy owner approves, so the record that matters is that documented exception: time-limited, with conditions such as isolation and monitoring, and a review. The risk owner's acceptance of what remains is recorded with it. A register entry accepting the risk is the runner-up: it records a real decision, but it is not the exception the policy requires.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the note records the policy owner's approval. But a shift-log note is informal; it is not a documented exception and sets no conditions or end date.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the risk owner's acceptance belongs in the record. But this policy requires the policy owner's approved exception, and a register entry is neither that exception nor its conditions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor knows the product. But support has ended, so no new flaws will be fixed, and a vendor cannot accept the organization's risk.

tips: Eliminate: A rests on an informal log note, and C on a vendor that no longer fixes the product; neither is a documented exception with conditions.
