Final two: D beats B because the policy requires an exception the policy owner approves; the risk owner's acceptance goes with it, but only the exception sets the conditions, expiry and review.
Exam cue: an unsupported system kept running against policy needs a documented, time-limited exception with conditions and a review, not a risk acceptance alone.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-22 (Unsupported System Components); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an unsupported system kept running needs a documented, time-limited exception with conditions and a review' (notes 5.4.3 End-of-Life Software and Devices). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A laundromat chain's system administrator plans to use a published Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmark as the secure baseline for its booking servers. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Apply every benchmark setting unchanged, trusting its expert authors
options.B: Start from installation defaults and add benchmark settings as needed
options.C: Tailor the benchmark to business needs, recording each deviation
options.D: Check servers once at build and record them as compliant

questions.key_concept: A published benchmark is a starting point: the organization tailors it to business needs, records each deviation and approves the result as its baseline.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a secure baseline is and what it has to fit.
questions.correct_explanation: Published benchmarks, such as the CIS Benchmarks, are trusted starting points, not finished baselines. The administrator adapts the settings to what the booking servers must do, records and justifies each deviation, and has the result approved as the baseline. Applying every setting unchanged is the runner-up: it seems safest, but some settings may break needed functions, and unrecorded workarounds then creep in as drift.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the benchmark is expert guidance. But it is written for general use; applied unchanged, some settings may break needed functions, and fixes then appear as unrecorded drift.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because defaults let servers go live fast. But defaults favor easy setup and are publicly known, so they are the starting point attackers expect.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a passed check feels final. But updates and quick fixes cause drift after build, so servers are scanned against the baseline regularly.

tips: Eliminate: B starts from installation defaults, which favor easy setup, and D checks only at build, though settings drift afterward.
Final two: C beats A because a benchmark is a starting point; tailoring it and recording each deviation gives an approved baseline that fits the business.
Exam cue: published benchmarks start a baseline; the organization tailors them, records deviations, approves the result and scans for drift.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-128 Section 3.2.1 (Establish Secure Configurations: common secure configurations such as CIS Benchmarks are a source, and deviations are justified and recorded); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-2 (Baseline Configuration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a published benchmark is tailored, deviations are recorded, and the result is approved as the baseline' (notes 5.4.4 Configuration Management and Secure Baselines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'/'record'. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: distractor A given the comma-ing shape the key has; 'vendor' taken off distractor B.

questions.question: A canoe club's billing software, used every day, gets a routine security update, and nothing suggests attackers are using the weakness it fixes. What should the IT technician do FIRST?

options.A: Test the update on a non-production copy, then schedule it
options.B: Install the update on the live billing server straight away
options.C: Skip it until attackers are seen using the weakness
options.D: Raise an emergency change to install it tonight

questions.key_concept: Routine patches are tested and scheduled through normal change management; the emergency route is for actively exploited or critical flaws.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the stem says about how urgent the flaw is.
questions.correct_explanation: Patches are tested before production so a fix does not break a service the office needs every day, then deployed through normal change management. Nothing suggests this flaw is being exploited, so the routine path fits. An emergency change is the runner-up: it is right for actively exploited flaws on exposed systems, but here it trades testing for speed the risk does not demand.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because quick patching closes flaws sooner. But an untested update can break billing the office uses daily, and production changes need approval.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because priority follows exploitation. But routine fixes still get applied on schedule; waiting for attacks leaves a known flaw open.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it does use the change process. But the emergency route suits actively exploited or critical flaws; a routine fix is tested and scheduled normally.

tips: Eliminate: B puts an untested update straight onto a daily-use system, and C leaves a known flaw open until attackers act.
Final two: A beats D because nothing shows active exploitation; emergency changes trade testing time for speed only when the risk demands it.
Exam cue: routine patch? Test, then schedule through change management. Actively exploited flaw on an exposed system? Use the emergency route.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-2 (Flaw Remediation); NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4 (Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning: Preventive Maintenance for Technology)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'routine patches are tested and scheduled; the emergency route is for actively exploited or critical flaws' (notes 5.4.5 Patch Management). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An esports team's IT technician is studying which changes its process treats as standard changes. Which change BEST fits that type?

options.A: Replacing a failed core firewall overnight to bring the network back
options.B: Adding a new payment provider after the change board approves it
options.C: Turning off logging on a slow database server to speed it up
options.D: Returning a drifted setting to its baseline by pre-approved steps

questions.key_concept: A standard change is low-risk and pre-approved by procedure; emergency changes get fast approval case by case, and other changes get full review.
questions.pre_read: Recall what sets the change types apart: risk, urgency and when approval happens.
questions.correct_explanation: A standard change is a low-risk, routine change whose steps a procedure approves in advance, such as returning a setting to its baseline; it can be made at once but is still recorded. Replacing a failed firewall overnight is the runner-up: it is also done fast, but it is an emergency change, approved case by case by a designated person and reviewed soon after.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: like a standard change, it happens quickly. But it is urgent and unplanned, so it is an emergency change, with fast approval by a designated person, then review.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the change board approves it. But new functionality reviewed case by case by the board is a full change, not one a procedure pre-approves.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it looks like a small setting change. But disabling logging weakens detection, so it needs full review, not a routine pre-approval.

tips: Eliminate: B adds new functionality that the board reviews case by case, and C weakens detection, so neither is a routine, pre-approved change.
Final two: D beats A because a standard change is routine and pre-approved by procedure; urgency makes A an emergency change, approved case by case.
Exam cue: standard means routine, low-risk and pre-approved; emergency means urgent with fast approval; anything else gets full review.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a standard change is low-risk, routine and pre-approved by procedure, unlike an emergency change' (notes 5.4.6 Change Management). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A heat-pump installer's security manager is planning its first red team exercise. Which team MOST accurately sets the rules of engagement, referees the exercise and can stop it if something goes wrong?

options.A: The white team, which oversees the exercise for both sides
options.B: The purple team, which joins red and blue into one group
options.C: The blue team, which defends the network during the exercise
options.D: The red team, which plays the attacker in the exercise

questions.key_concept: The white team sets the rules, referees, confirms test activity and can stop an exercise; purple teaming is red and blue cooperating.
questions.pre_read: Recall the job of each team color in an exercise.
questions.correct_explanation: The white team sets the rules of engagement, referees, confirms whether activity is part of the test and can halt the exercise if real operations are at risk. Purple is the runner-up: it sounds like a neutral middle team, but purple teaming is red and blue working together and sharing findings in real time, not an independent referee.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: purple sits between red and blue. But purple teaming is red and blue sharing findings to improve detection, not a referee that can stop the test.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because defenders protect live systems. But the blue team defends as normal and may not even know the exercise is running.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the red team plans the attack. But a team cannot referee its own attack; independent oversight keeps the test within scope.

tips: Eliminate: C defends and may not know a test is running, and D is the attacker, which cannot referee its own exercise.
Final two: A beats B because purple teaming is red and blue cooperating; the white team is the independent referee that can stop the exercise.
Exam cue: red attacks, blue defends, purple is red and blue sharing in real time, and white referees, confirms tests and can stop them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSRC Glossary (White Team: referees an engagement between a red team and a blue team and enforces the exercise rules, per CNSSI 4009-2022); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-8(2) (Penetration Testing | Red Team Exercises)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the white team sets the rules, referees and can stop an exercise; purple is red and blue cooperating' (notes 5.5.1 Red, Blue and Purple Teams). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A luggage maker's analyst wants a flaw's Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0 score to reflect that the affected server holds card data and faces the internet. Which metric group BEST fits?

options.A: The Base metric group
options.B: The Environmental metric group
options.C: The Threat metric group
options.D: The Supplemental metric group

questions.key_concept: CVSS 4.0 Environmental metrics tailor a score to the affected system's importance and setting; Base describes the flaw, and Threat its exploitation.
questions.pre_read: Recall the four CVSS 4.0 metric groups and what each describes.
questions.correct_explanation: CVSS 4.0 has four metric groups. Base describes the flaw itself, the same for everyone; Threat adjusts for exploit maturity; Environmental tailors the score to the consumer's setting, such as how much confidentiality matters on this system and how exposed it is; Supplemental adds context without changing the score. Threat is the runner-up: it concerns attacker activity, not the importance of this server.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because Base is the score most often quoted. But it describes the flaw as published, the same for every organization, so it cannot reflect this server.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Threat metrics also refine the score for the consumer. But they cover exploit maturity, such as active attacks, not how important or exposed this server is.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the server's details are extra context. But Supplemental metrics do not change the score at all, so the server's importance would not count.

tips: Eliminate: A describes the flaw the same way for everyone, and D adds context without changing the score; neither can reflect this server.
Final two: B beats C because Threat covers exploit maturity, while the server's importance and exposure belong to the Environmental group.
Exam cue: in CVSS 4.0, Base is the flaw, Threat is attacker activity, Environmental is your system, and Supplemental is context with no score change.
questions.framework_ref: FIRST Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 Specification Document Section 4 (Environmental Metrics: customize the score to the importance of the affected asset and the controls in place); FIRST Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 Specification Document Section 1 (Introduction)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'CVSS 4.0 Environmental metrics tailor a score to the affected system's importance and setting' (notes 5.5.2 Vulnerability Scanning and Penetration Testing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A picture-framing chain needs each system owner's approval before scanning, and its analyst finds 15 new inventory servers absent from the scan list. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the owners of the 15 servers to approve adding them
options.B: Add the 15 to tonight's scan and tell their owners afterward
options.C: Treat the 15 as covered, since they copy an approved server build
options.D: Run a penetration test on the 15 servers in place of scanning

questions.key_concept: Vulnerability scan coverage should match the asset inventory, and adding systems to the scans still needs each system owner's approval first.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the procedure requires before any server is scanned.
questions.correct_explanation: Scan coverage should match the inventory, so the 15 servers need adding, but the procedure requires each owner's approval before any system is scanned. The analyst asks the owners first, then adds them. Adding them to tonight's scan is the runner-up: it closes the gap fastest, but scanning without approval breaks the procedure and can disrupt services the owners have not planned for.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the servers do need scanning. But the procedure requires owner approval first, and an unplanned scan can disrupt a service its owner has not prepared.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the servers share an approved build. But settings, software and exposure drift apart after build, so only scanning each one shows its flaws.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a penetration test goes deeper. But it is more intrusive than a scan and needs the owners' approval and scope just the same.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes a shared build means identical flaws, and D swaps in a more intrusive test that needs the same approval.
Final two: A beats B because the procedure needs owner approval before scanning; closing the coverage gap still starts with that approval.
Exam cue: compare scan coverage with the inventory, and get the system owner's approval before testing anything new, even inside your own organization.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-5 (Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning); NIST SP 800-115 Section 6.5 (Assessment Plan Development: the plan states the type and level of testing permitted)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'scan coverage should match the inventory, and adding systems still needs owner approval first' (notes 5.5.2 Vulnerability Scanning and Penetration Testing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An animal shelter's volunteer developer used the shelter's approved AI coding assistant to write the adoption form's input handling and wants to skip static analysis. Which response is BEST for the security analyst to give?

options.A: Run the same static analysis as for every other code change
options.B: Skip static analysis for code from an approved assistant
options.C: Review the form's open-source libraries for known flaws instead
options.D: Run dynamic testing on a staging copy instead of static analysis

questions.key_concept: Code from AI coding assistants gets the same static analysis and review as any other code, because assistants can suggest insecure patterns.
questions.pre_read: Recall what static analysis looks for and when it runs.
questions.correct_explanation: Code from an AI coding assistant is code like any other: assistants learn from public code, insecure patterns included, and can suggest unsafe input handling. It gets the same static analysis and review before release. Checking the form's open-source libraries is the runner-up: it is sound practice, but it covers code others wrote, not the input handling the assistant produced.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the shelter did approve the assistant. But approval settles who may use the tool and with what data; it does not make any given output secure.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: checking libraries for known flaws is sound practice. But the risk here is the input handling the assistant wrote, which only analysis of that code can check.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because dynamic testing on a staging copy finds runtime flaws safely. But it probes the running form from outside, so it adds to static analysis rather than replacing it.

tips: Eliminate: B treats approving the tool as proof its output is secure, and D swaps static analysis for runtime testing, which never examines the code itself.
Final two: A beats C because library checks cover code others wrote; the input handling the assistant wrote needs its own static analysis and review.
Exam cue: AI-written code gets the same testing and review as human-written code. Who or what wrote it never lowers the bar.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-11(1) (Developer Testing and Evaluation | Static Code Analysis); NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF v1.1) PW.7.2 (perform the code review and/or code analysis based on the organization's secure coding standards and record and triage all discovered issues)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'code from AI coding assistants gets the same static analysis and review as any other code' (notes 5.5.3 Static and Dynamic Application Testing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and' (now 'every'); distractor B without 'since'/'is'.

questions.subtopic: 5.5 Security testing. Responding to modeled threats
questions.question: Threat modeling a pet-sitting app's design, the team proposes leaving one low-impact threat unfixed, within the organization's tolerance. Which step should the security analyst propose as BEST for that threat?

options.A: Leave the threat off the log, since no fix is planned
options.B: Record the risk owner's acceptance in the threat log
options.C: Record it as open for the system owner to fix later
options.D: Ask the penetration testers to confirm it after launch

questions.key_concept: Each threat found in threat modeling gets a response; one left unfixed within tolerance needs the risk owner's recorded acceptance.
questions.pre_read: Recall the responses a threat model can give each threat, and who decides each one.
questions.correct_explanation: Every threat a model finds gets a response: a control, a design change or documented acceptance. Within tolerance, acceptance is the risk owner's decision, so the analyst has the risk owner accept it and records that in the threat log. Recording it as open for the system owner to fix later is the runner-up: it keeps a record, but plans a fix the team does not intend, and no one has accepted the risk meanwhile.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because no work is planned for it. But an unrecorded threat is forgotten, and nobody with authority has accepted the risk it leaves.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the threat stays on record with an owner. But a fix penciled in for later is not a decision; leaving it unfixed needs the risk owner's recorded acceptance.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because testers can check whether it is real. But it moves a design decision past launch and still leaves no one accountable for the risk.

tips: Eliminate: A drops the threat from the log, and D pushes a design decision to testing after launch; neither gives the threat an approved response.
Final two: B beats C because a threat left unfixed needs the risk owner's recorded acceptance; an open item marked for a later fix is a plan no one has decided.
Exam cue: every modeled threat ends with a control, a design change or recorded acceptance by the risk owner, within tolerance.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-7 (Risk Response); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-11(2) (Developer Testing and Evaluation | Threat Modeling and Vulnerability Analyses)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'every modeled threat gets a response; one left unfixed needs the risk owner's recorded acceptance' (notes 5.5.4 Threat Modeling). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 5.5 Security testing. Testing an autonomous AI agent
questions.question: In an authorized test, a hydroelectric utility checks its new AI security agent, which can isolate servers on its own. Which result should the security analyst report as MOST serious?

options.A: The agent took four minutes to isolate a test server
options.B: The agent's alert summaries used confusing technical terms
options.C: The agent kept isolating a server after staff tried to stop it
options.D: The agent wrongly flagged two harmless servers in one week

questions.key_concept: AI tools allowed to act alone, such as automatic containment, must let a person stop them; a missing override outranks accuracy or speed problems.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the agent can do without asking anyone.
questions.correct_explanation: AI tools that act on their own need a person able to stop them. If staff cannot halt the agent, any mistake, such as isolating a server the plant needs, runs to completion, and at a power utility that can disrupt operations. The false alarms are the runner-up: they need tuning, but while people can override the agent, a wrong isolation can be stopped and reversed before it does lasting harm.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because response speed matters. But four minutes still contains the threat, and speed can be tuned; it is not a loss of control.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because unclear summaries slow analysts down. But it is a usability problem that training or settings fix, not a safety gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: false alarms could lead to wrong isolations. But they are expected and tunable while staff can override; without an override, every error is unstoppable.

tips: Eliminate: A is a speed issue that still ends in containment, and B is a usability issue; neither takes control away from people.
Final two: C beats D because false flags can be tuned and caught while people can override; with no override, any wrong action runs to completion.
Exam cue: when an AI tool can act on its own, test first whether a person can stop it, especially where operations are critical.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 2.4 (mechanisms are in place and responsibilities assigned to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI systems that perform inconsistently with intended use); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 4.1 (post-deployment monitoring plans, including capturing user input, appeal and override)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI tools that take high-impact actions must let a person stop them' (notes 5.5.6 Testing AI-Integrated Defenses). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A ride maker's data loss prevention (DLP) tool blocks outgoing files labeled Confidential, yet an unlabeled copy of a Confidential ride design left by email. What does this MOST accurately show the security analyst?

options.A: Labeling the copy would have set its classification level
options.B: The DLP tool needs to set file levels in place of owners
options.C: Labels encrypt files, so the unlabeled copy left unprotected
options.D: The tool enforces handling by label, so every copy needs one

questions.key_concept: A label makes the owner's classification visible to people and tools; a label-based DLP rule can act only on data that carries the label.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a classification decides and what a label adds.
questions.correct_explanation: Classification is the owner's decision; the label is how people and tools see it. This DLP rule acts on labels, so a copy without one looks like ordinary data and leaves unchecked, though its level is still Confidential. Letting the tool set levels is the runner-up: automatic tools can suggest labels, but the data owner's decision governs, and the gap here was a missing label, not a missing decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because labeling and classifying often happen together. But the owner decides the level and the label only records it, so labeling never sets a level.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: tools can suggest labels for unlabeled copies. But the data owner sets the level; what failed here was a copy missing its label, not who decided.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the labeled files were stopped. But a label is a mark, not encryption; the DLP tool stopped those files by reading the label, not by any cipher.

tips: Eliminate: A and C both misread labels: owners decide the level and a label only records it, and a label is a mark, not encryption.
Final two: D beats B because the owner had already set the level; what failed was a copy missing the label the tool reads.
Exam cue: classification is the decision and labeling makes it visible; label-based tools can enforce only what a label shows.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-16 (Security and Privacy Attributes); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.12 (Data leakage prevention)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'labels make the owner's classification visible so tools such as DLP can enforce handling' (notes 5.1.1 Data Classification and Labeling). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A broadband provider's system masks bank account numbers as it displays them, so call-center agents see only the last four digits. Which statement about the stored records should the security analyst give as MOST accurate?

options.A: The stored records now keep only the last four digits
options.B: The stored records still hold full numbers to protect
options.C: The stored records hold vault tokens in place of the numbers
options.D: The stored records are encrypted under each agent's own key

questions.key_concept: Dynamic masking changes only what a viewer sees; the stored values are unchanged and still need full protection.
questions.pre_read: Recall how static masking, dynamic masking and tokenization differ.
questions.correct_explanation: Masking data as it is displayed changes only what the viewer sees; the database still holds every full account number. Those stored numbers need the same protection as before, such as access control and encryption at rest. Believing the records now hold only four digits is the runner-up: that describes a changed copy made by static masking, not a mask applied on display.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: some masking does change stored data, as in a masked test copy. But this system masks on display, so the stored numbers are untouched.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because tokens also hide real values. But tokenization replaces stored values with tokens; a display mask leaves the real numbers in place.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because encryption protects stored data. But masking is not encryption, and hiding digits on screens says nothing about how records are encrypted.

tips: Eliminate: C describes tokenization, which replaces stored values, and D describes encryption; masking on display is neither.
Final two: B beats A because masking on display changes only the view; the full numbers stay in the records and still need protection.
Exam cue: dynamic masking hides data from the viewer, not from the database; protect the stored values in full.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'dynamic masking changes only the view; stored values still need full protection' (notes 5.1.3 Data Masking and Tokenization). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A tile wholesaler's disposal vendor reports that it degaussed 30 laptop solid-state drives (SSDs), and every run finished without errors. What should the system administrator conclude as MOST accurate?

options.A: The drives are sanitized, since every degaussing run completed
options.B: The drives are destroyed, since degaussing ruins any drive
options.C: The drives are not sanitized, since degaussing cannot erase flash
options.D: The drives are sanitized once the vendor issues its certificate

questions.key_concept: Sanitization must suit the media; degaussing can complete on an SSD yet leave its flash data recoverable, so purge or destroy instead.
questions.pre_read: Recall how degaussing works and which kind of storage it affects.
questions.correct_explanation: Degaussing uses a magnetic field, which erases magnetic disks but does nothing to the flash chips in an SSD. A run can finish without errors and still leave every file recoverable, so these drives are not sanitized; they need a purge, such as the drive's sanitize command, or destruction. Waiting for the vendor's certificate is the runner-up: a certificate records the method used but cannot make an unsuitable method work.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the runs reported no errors. But a finished run shows only that the degausser ran; magnets do not affect the flash chips that hold the data.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because degaussing often ruins magnetic hard disks. But SSDs store data in flash chips, which magnets leave intact, so both the drives and the data survive.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a certificate of sanitization should record each drive. But it documents the method used; it cannot turn an unsuitable method into a sanitized drive.

tips: Eliminate: A takes a finished run as proof, and B assumes degaussing ruins any drive; magnets do not affect the flash chips inside SSDs.
Final two: C beats D because a certificate records what was done; it cannot make degaussing work on flash, so the drives still hold data.
Exam cue: match the sanitization method to the media, and judge the outcome, not just whether the tool ran.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 Section 4.5.2 (Sanitization Validation: degaussing an SSD can complete successfully, yet no sensitive data is sanitized); NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 Section 3.1 (Sanitization Methods: clear, purge and destroy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a sanitization method must suit the media; a completed degaussing run leaves SSD data intact' (notes 5.1.4 Media Sanitization: Clear, Purge and Destroy). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: role IT technician -> system administrator. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: distractor B no longer says the same thing twice (blind tester flag).

questions.question: A pension fund signs its member-portal software updates with RSA, and its system administrator says quantum risk covers these signatures, not only encrypted data. Which reply should the security analyst give as MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree, since quantum attacks could forge RSA signatures as well
options.B: Disagree, since signatures guard no secrets an attacker could steal
options.C: Agree, though longer RSA keys would keep signing quantum-safe
options.D: Disagree, since the risk lies in the SHA-256 hash rather than RSA

questions.key_concept: Quantum risk covers digital signatures as well as key exchange: RSA and elliptic curve signatures must move to post-quantum standards.
questions.pre_read: Recall which algorithms a large quantum computer would break.
questions.correct_explanation: A large quantum computer would break RSA and elliptic curve methods in both their jobs: key exchange and digital signatures. Forged signatures could make malicious updates look genuine, so NIST's transition plan retires quantum-vulnerable signatures too, in favor of post-quantum signature standards. Disagreeing because signatures hide no secrets is the runner-up: signatures protect integrity and origin, and forgery breaks exactly that.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: signatures hide no data that could be stolen. But a quantum computer could forge RSA signatures, letting an attacker sign malicious updates the portal would trust.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because longer keys often add strength. But a large quantum computer breaks RSA at any practical key size, so signing must move to post-quantum algorithms.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because every signature uses a hash. But hashes such as SHA-256 are far less affected by quantum attacks; the RSA signing step is what breaks.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts longer RSA keys, which do not resist quantum attack, and D blames the hash, though hashes are far less affected.
Final two: A beats B because a quantum computer could forge RSA signatures and sign malicious updates; NIST's transition retires quantum-vulnerable signatures too.
Exam cue: quantum risk hits public-key cryptography in both its jobs, key exchange and signatures; symmetric ciphers and hashes are far less affected.
questions.framework_ref: NIST FIPS 203 Section 1.2 (Context: large-scale quantum computers would put public-key key establishment and signatures at risk); NIST IR 8547 Section 4.1.1 (Digital Signatures: quantum-vulnerable RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA signatures are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'quantum risk covers digital signatures as well as key exchange' (notes 5.1.7 Quantum-Resistant Cryptography). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 5.1 Data security. Controls for public AI use
questions.question: Despite training on its AI policy, a property valuation firm's staff keep uploading client valuation files labeled Confidential to free public chatbots. Which control should the security analyst propose as BEST to stop this?

options.A: Data loss prevention rules that block the labeled files at upload
options.B: A second, longer round of AI policy training for all staff
options.C: A rule that staff clear their chatbot histories after each session
options.D: Removal of client names from labeled files before any upload

questions.key_concept: When training alone fails, data loss prevention that reads labels can block sensitive data headed to unapproved AI services.
questions.pre_read: Recall the main kinds of control that can limit data leaving through AI tools.
questions.correct_explanation: Training is already in place and has not changed behavior, so a technical control is needed. Data loss prevention can read the Confidential label and warn or block when those files head to unapproved AI sites, stopping the disclosure before it happens. More training is the runner-up: awareness still matters, but repeating a control that has already failed does not stop the next upload.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: training is part of any AI policy. But staff have been trained and keep uploading; repeating it adds no barrier at the moment of disclosure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes visible traces. But the provider may already have stored or logged the uploaded files; clearing history does not undo the disclosure.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because names are the obvious identifiers. But valuations still identify clients by address and price, and no stripping makes an unapproved public chatbot acceptable.

tips: Eliminate: C clears the user's view while the provider keeps its copies, and D strips names while the files still identify clients.
Final two: A beats B because training has already failed here; a technical control that reads labels stops the data as it leaves.
Exam cue: when an administrative control keeps failing, add a technical control that enforces the same rule.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.12 (Data leakage prevention); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'when training fails, DLP that reads labels blocks sensitive data headed to public AI services' (notes 5.1.8 Data Leakage into Public AI Services). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Length evened out (4 Nov 2026, blind re-test): the key is no longer the lone longest or shortest option by a wide margin. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'those'; now carries 'the'.

questions.question: A parking app's sign-in log records only the time and the words 'login failed' for each failed attempt. Which addition should the security analyst request as MOST useful for investigations?

options.A: Keeping the same attempt entries for five years, not one
options.B: The account name and source address of every attempt
options.C: Encrypting each log file where it is stored on the server
options.D: Logging every function the app runs at debug level

questions.key_concept: Useful log entries record who acted, what happened, when, from where and the result, so investigators can trace activity.
questions.pre_read: Recall which details a useful log entry should hold.
questions.correct_explanation: A useful log entry shows who did what, when, from where and with what result. These entries have the time and result but no account or source address, so no one can tell one user's typo from an attack spread across many accounts or launched from one address. Keeping entries longer is the runner-up: retention matters, but five years of entries without names or addresses still answer nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: logs must be kept long enough for investigations. But longer retention keeps the same thin entries; it adds no account or address to work with.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because logs need protection. But encryption guards the file's confidentiality; it adds no detail about who tried to sign in or from where.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because more logging sounds more thorough. But debug output floods the log with noise and still may not record who tried to sign in, or from where.

tips: Eliminate: C protects the log without adding detail, and D adds noise rather than the facts an investigation needs.
Final two: B beats A because keeping thin entries longer does not make them useful; each entry needs the account and the source.
Exam cue: a good log entry answers who, what, when, where and with what result.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-3 (Content of Audit Records); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'useful log entries record who, what, when, where and the result' (notes 5.2.2 Logging and Monitoring). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 5.2 Security operations. Checking AI case summaries
questions.question: A mining company's AI case summary says a malicious file on a laptop was quarantined, but the laptop's endpoint log shows no quarantine. What should the security analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Close the case, since the summary reports the file quarantined
options.B: Have the AI tool reread the log and redraft its summary
options.C: Treat the file as active, since the log shows no quarantine
options.D: Report the faulty summary to the AI tool's provider at once

questions.key_concept: AI case summaries can state facts the logs do not support; analysts check the evidence and act on what the logs show.
questions.pre_read: Think about how an AI tool produces a case summary.
questions.correct_explanation: AI summaries can state facts the logs do not support, so the evidence wins: with no quarantine recorded, the analyst treats the file as still active and acts on the endpoint log. Reporting the faulty summary to the vendor is the runner-up: the error should reach the vendor through the tool's owner, but doing that first leaves a possibly live threat on the laptop.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the summary is specific. But AI summaries can state things that never happened; closing on it leaves a possibly active file on the laptop.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a fresh draft might be right. But a second AI answer is still unverified, and the endpoint log already shows what happened.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the faulty summary should be reported so the tool improves. But that goes through the tool's owner and can wait; a file that may still be active cannot.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts the summary over the record, and B asks the same tool to settle its own error; neither acts on the evidence.
Final two: C beats D because the possibly active file comes first; the tool's error is reported afterward, through the tool's owner.
Exam cue: when an AI summary and the logs disagree, the logs are the evidence; act on them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) Section 2.2 (Confabulation: confidently presented erroneous or false content); NIST CSF 2.0 DE.AE-02 (potentially adverse events are analyzed to better understand associated activities)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI summaries can state facts the logs do not support; act on the evidence' (notes 5.2.4 AI-Driven Correlation and Alert Fatigue). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. questions.subtopic: 5.2 Security operations. Threat frameworks for AI
questions.question: A public broadcaster's security team is planning a test of its machine learning comment-moderation model and wants documented examples of how attackers have fooled or stolen models. Which resource BEST meets this need?

options.A: MITRE ATT&CK, the matrix of tactics and techniques seen in real intrusions
options.B: MITRE ATLAS, the knowledge base drawn from real-world case studies
options.C: The NIST AI RMF, a framework for governing and managing AI risk
options.D: The Cyber Kill Chain, which orders an intrusion's seven stages

questions.key_concept: MITRE ATLAS is ATT&CK's companion knowledge base of real attacker tactics and techniques against AI systems, used to plan AI tests.
questions.pre_read: Recall the knowledge bases that describe real attacker behavior.
questions.correct_explanation: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems) is a public knowledge base of attacker tactics and techniques aimed at AI, such as evading or stealing models, with real case studies, so it suits planning this test. ATT&CK is the runner-up: it is the same style of map, but it covers intrusions into enterprise IT, not methods aimed at the models themselves.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: ATT&CK maps real attacker techniques the same way. But its matrix covers intrusions into IT systems; methods aimed at AI models are cataloged in ATLAS.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is built for AI. But the AI RMF guides how an organization governs and manages AI risk; it does not catalog attacks on models.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it describes how attacks unfold. But it is a general seven-stage model of intrusions, with no catalog of methods used against AI models.

tips: Eliminate: C governs AI risk without cataloging attacks, and D orders the general stages of an intrusion; neither lists methods aimed at AI models.
Final two: B beats A because ATT&CK maps intrusions into IT systems, while ATLAS, its companion, catalogs attacks on AI models with real case studies.
Exam cue: for attacker techniques against IT systems, think ATT&CK; for attacks on AI and machine learning models, think ATLAS.
questions.framework_ref: MITRE ATLAS knowledge base (Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems: tactics, techniques and case studies of attacks on AI systems); NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 2.2.4 (Evasion Attacks in the Real World: further evasion attacks on malware classifiers are cataloged in the MITRE ATLAS knowledge base)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'MITRE ATLAS catalogs attacker techniques against AI systems, as ATT&CK does for enterprise IT' (notes 5.2.7 Threat Frameworks: MITRE ATT&CK and the Kill Chain). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and', now 'the' like the distractors.

questions.question: A cinema chain's system administrator restored its booking server from a backup made before an intrusion was detected, then patched the exploited flaw. Which step should the incident response team take FIRST before reopening it?

options.A: Check the restored server for any signs of compromise
options.B: Hold the lessons learned review with the whole team
options.C: Treat it as clean, since the backup predates the detected attack
options.D: Wipe the original server's disk, as the restored copy replaces it

questions.key_concept: Before a restored system returns to production, responders check it for signs of compromise, since backups can carry an attacker's foothold.
questions.pre_read: Recall where the recovery phase starts and where it ends.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery returns systems to trusted operation, so a restored server is checked for signs of compromise, such as unknown accounts or scheduled tasks, before it goes live. Treating it as clean because the backup predates the detection is the runner-up: attackers are often inside long before anyone notices, so a backup made before detection can still carry their foothold, and its date proves nothing.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because lessons should be captured. But the full review comes once recovery is done, and it cannot show whether this restored server is clean.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the backup predates the detection. But attackers are often inside before anyone notices, so the backup may hold their foothold; checking comes first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the old disk looks useless now. But it is evidence of the intrusion, and wiping it may break the plan's evidence rules.

tips: Eliminate: B holds the full lessons learned review, which comes after recovery, and D wipes evidence the investigation may still need.
Final two: A beats C because a backup's date cannot prove it is clean; attackers are often inside before detection, so the restored server is checked first.
Exam cue: in recovery, confirm restored systems are clean before returning them to production.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Table 3 (RC.RP-05: check restored assets for indicators of compromise and remediate root causes before production use); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-10 (System Recovery and Reconstitution)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'restored systems are checked for signs of compromise before returning to production' (notes 5.3.2 The Incident Response Lifecycle and CSF 2.0). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An attacker used an unpatched plugin to plant a web shell on a crafts marketplace's server; the system administrator deleted it, and a full scan found nothing else. What MOST remains to complete eradication?

options.A: Restore the server and all its plugins from last night's backup
options.B: Monitor the server closely for signs of the attacker
options.C: Patch the vulnerable plugin the attacker used to get in
options.D: Power off the server until the lessons learned review

questions.key_concept: Eradication removes the attacker's tools and closes the weakness they used; deleting malware alone leaves the way back in.
questions.pre_read: Recall what eradication must remove besides the attacker's files.
questions.correct_explanation: Eradication removes the cause of an incident, not just what the attacker left behind. With the web shell gone but the plugin still unpatched, the attacker can come straight back the same way, so closing that flaw, with resetting any exposed credentials, finishes the job. Closer monitoring is the runner-up: it can spot a return, but it leaves the entry point open.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because restoring is how recovery starts. But last night's backup still has the unpatched plugin and may hold the attacker's files; eradication is not done.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: close monitoring can spot the attacker coming back. But it only detects a return; the unpatched plugin still lets them in, so eradication is not complete.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because an offline server cannot be attacked. But powering off delays the work without removing the cause; the flaw is still there when it restarts.

tips: Eliminate: A restores a copy that still has the flaw, and D switches the server off without removing the cause.
Final two: C beats B because eradication must close the way in; monitoring would only watch the attacker reuse the plugin flaw.
Exam cue: eradication is complete only when the root cause, such as the exploited flaw, is fixed on every affected system.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Table 3 (RS.MI-02: eradication eliminates persistence mechanisms and entry points, including all exploited vulnerabilities); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-2 (Flaw Remediation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'eradication closes the exploited weakness as well as removing the attacker's tools' (notes 5.3.3 Containment, Eradication and Recovery). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 5.3 Incident response. Containing a data exposure
questions.question: A sports league's playbook lets its on-call security analyst revoke public links during data exposures; a Restricted contracts folder is publicly shared, and its data owner is mid-flight. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Report it to the data owner and wait until they land
options.B: Delete the folder so that no outside party can open it
options.C: Rename the folder so its public link is harder to find
options.D: Delete the public link, then report it to the data owner

questions.key_concept: When a playbook assigns a containment step to the practitioner, they act at once within it and inform the owner afterward.
questions.pre_read: Recall the goal of short-term containment.
questions.correct_explanation: The playbook gives the on-call analyst authority to revoke public links during an exposure, so deleting the link, which revokes it, is in role and happens at once; while it stays live, anyone can copy the Restricted contracts. The owner is then told what was done. Reporting to the owner and waiting is the runner-up: owners decide about their data, but here the procedure has already assigned this step to the analyst.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the data owner decides how their data is handled. But the playbook already gives this step to the analyst, and waiting out a flight keeps the exposure open.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because deleting ends the exposure fast. But deleting the whole folder destroys business records and evidence, goes beyond the playbook, and cannot recall copies already taken.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a new name seems to hide the folder. But a sharing link keeps working after a rename; hiding is not the same as removing access.

tips: Eliminate: B deletes the whole folder, destroying records and evidence beyond what containment needs, and C renames it, but a sharing link keeps working after a rename.
Final two: D beats A because the playbook gives the analyst this step; the owner is informed, not waited for, while the exposure grows.
Exam cue: when procedure assigns a containment step to you, do it and inform the owner; escalate what is outside your authority.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.MI-01 (incidents are contained); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'when the playbook assigns a containment step, the practitioner acts and informs the owner' (notes 5.3.3 Containment, Eradication and Recovery). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 5.3 Incident response. Channels for incident data
questions.question: During a wine merchant's breach investigation, a remote responder cannot reach the restricted case folder, and a colleague offers to email the firewall logs to the responder's personal account. What should the responder do FIRST?

options.A: Accept, then delete the email once the analysis is finished
options.B: Accept the logs if they arrive in a password-protected archive
options.C: Decline, and ask the incident response lead to restore access
options.D: Decline the email, then ask for the logs by personal chat

questions.key_concept: Incident data keeps its handling rules: it stays in approved systems and reaches only authorized people, even when access is inconvenient.
questions.pre_read: Recall how classification and handling rules apply to incident data.
questions.correct_explanation: Incident data can hold sensitive details, so it stays inside approved systems and goes only to authorized people; a personal account is outside the organization's control and creates a new exposure. The responder declines and asks the incident response lead to restore access. A password-protected archive is the runner-up: it adds some protection, but the logs still land in an account the organization cannot manage, monitor or wipe.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because deleting seems to undo the risk. But copies stay with the mail provider and in sent items; the data has already left approved systems.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a password adds protection in transit. But the logs still end up in a personal account the organization cannot control, monitor or wipe.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because chat feels quick and private. But a personal chat app is another unapproved channel, outside the organization's control, like personal email.

tips: Eliminate: A and D both send incident data through personal channels; deleting afterward or switching apps does not keep it in approved systems.
Final two: C beats B because a password does not change where the logs end up; only restored, approved access keeps them under control.
Exam cue: incident data keeps its handling rules; when the approved route fails, fix access instead of routing around it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Table 3 (RS.AN-06: incident response records can contain sensitive information and are safeguarded, with access for authorized personnel only); NIST CSF 2.0 RS.CO-03 (information is shared with designated internal and external stakeholders)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'incident data stays in approved systems even when access is inconvenient' (notes 5.3.5 Data Handling During an Incident). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A garden center's unencrypted USB stick of staff records was lost, then found within an hour with nothing exposed; a manager says no review is needed. Which response is BEST for the incident response lead?

options.A: Agree, since no data left the company and no harm was done
options.B: Hold a short review to find out who lost the stick
options.C: Hold a brief review of why the stick was never encrypted
options.D: Remind all staff that unencrypted sticks break the media policy

questions.key_concept: Even small incidents get a short lessons learned review, because they expose the same gaps as large ones at lower cost.
questions.pre_read: Recall which incidents a lessons learned review covers and what it looks for.
questions.correct_explanation: Small incidents often reveal the same gaps as big ones, at far lower cost. Here the stick held staff records unencrypted, so a short review asks how that was possible and assigns a fix, such as enforced encryption on removable media. A policy reminder is the runner-up: it may help, but without finding why the stick was unencrypted, the same gap waits for a loss that is not recovered.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because nothing was exposed. But luck, not a control, prevented harm; the gap that let staff records sit unencrypted on a stick is still open.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because someone did lose the stick. But reviews look for gaps in process and tools, not for blame, which teaches staff to hide future losses.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a reminder costs little. But it repeats the rule without finding why the stick was unencrypted, so the real gap may stay open.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a lucky outcome as no problem, and B aims the review at a person, though reviews look for process and tool gaps.
Final two: C beats D because a reminder repeats the rule; a review finds why the data was unencrypted and assigns a fix.
Exam cue: review small incidents too; they expose the same gaps as big ones at a lower cost.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.IM-03 (improvements are identified from execution of operational processes, procedures, and activities)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'small incidents still get a lessons learned review that looks for the gap' (notes 5.3.6 Lessons Learned and Continuous Improvement). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'short'/'how' (now 'encrypted'); distractor B now 'short'.

questions.question: Midway through a cruise booking agency's phishing tabletop, the facilitator announces that the attacker has now signed in as the payroll manager and asks the team what changes. What is this announcement MOST accurately called?

options.A: Drill, a separate hands-on practice of one specific response task
options.B: Functional exercise, as the team now performs recovery
options.C: Change of scope, needing the exercise sponsor's approval
options.D: Inject, a scripted development testing how the team adapts

questions.key_concept: An inject is a planned new development a facilitator adds during an exercise to test how the team adapts its decisions.
questions.pre_read: Recall how a facilitator moves a tabletop scenario forward.
questions.correct_explanation: An inject is a planned, scripted development the facilitator adds during an exercise, such as a new attacker move, to see how the team adapts its decisions. It is part of the scenario design, so the exercise stays a tabletop within its agreed scope. Calling it a change of scope is the runner-up: the facts changed, but injects are planned inside the scope from the start.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the team must respond to something new. But a drill is a separate hands-on practice of one task; this team is still discussing the scenario.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the scenario has moved on. But a functional exercise means carrying out duties in a simulated environment; here the team is still only talking.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the scenario's facts did change. But injects are planned into the scenario in advance, so the scope and objectives stay the same and need no new approval.

tips: Eliminate: A is a separate practice of one task, and B means carrying out steps in a simulated environment; this team is still talking.
Final two: D beats C because injects are planned parts of the scenario, inside the agreed scope; they test adaptation without changing what the exercise covers.
Exam cue: a new development the facilitator adds mid-exercise is an inject; it tests decisions, not systems.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-84 Section 4 (Tabletop Exercises: discussion-based events); NIST SP 800-84 Section 5.3 (Develop the Functional Exercise Material: a message inject is a pre-scripted message provided to participants during an exercise)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an inject is a planned new fact a facilitator adds to test how the team adapts' (notes 5.3.7 Incident Response Exercises and Tabletops). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A hostel chain's asset inventory lists its new AI translation service only by name and monthly cost. Which added detail BEST helps the security team decide how much protection the service needs?

options.A: The contract renewal date and the vendor's billing contact
options.B: The version of the AI model the vendor currently runs
options.C: The names of every staff member who has used the service
options.D: The kinds of guest data it handles and its criticality

questions.key_concept: Inventory entries record each asset's data and criticality, AI services included, so protection can match what is at stake.
questions.pre_read: Recall what an asset inventory entry should record.
questions.correct_explanation: Protection follows the value and sensitivity of what an asset touches. Recording the data types the service handles, such as guests' passport details, and how critical it is to daily work tells the team which classification and controls apply. The model version is the runner-up: it helps track vendor changes and retest after updates, but it says little about the harm a breach of the service would cause.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because inventories often track contracts. But renewal and billing details support purchasing; they say nothing about how sensitive the service's data is.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: version tracking helps spot model changes. But a version number does not show what data is at stake or how much the business depends on it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because users matter for access reviews. But a list of past users does not show how sensitive the data is or how critical the service is.

tips: Eliminate: A records purchasing details and C records past users; neither shows what is at stake if the service is breached.
Final two: D beats B because data types and criticality set the protection level; a version number tracks change, not value.
Exam cue: an inventory entry that drives protection names the owner, the data handled and the criticality, for AI services as for servers.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.6 (mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-05 (assets are prioritized based on classification, criticality, resources and impact on the mission)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'inventory entries for AI services record the data handled and the criticality' (notes 5.4.1 Asset Inventory and Ownership). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A tax preparation office's multifunction printer, whose drive holds scanned client ID documents, is going to the vendor's depot for a two-week repair. Which step is BEST for the help desk technician before shipping it?

options.A: Delete the scans from its drive and record the step
options.B: Set a new admin password or PIN on its menu before shipping
options.C: Ship it unchanged, since the printer will come back afterward
options.D: Sanitize or remove the drive before shipping the printer

questions.key_concept: Equipment leaving for off-site repair has its storage sanitized or removed first, even though the device will come back.
questions.pre_read: Recall when data on a device leaves the organization's control.
questions.correct_explanation: Data leaves the organization's control whenever the device does, and a two-week repair puts the scanned ID documents in outside hands. So the drive is sanitized or kept back before shipping, and the step is recorded in the maintenance records. Deleting the scans is the runner-up: it looks like removing them, but deleted files stay recoverable on the drive.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: deleting looks like removing the scans, and the step is recorded. But deleting only removes the file entries; the scans stay recoverable on the drive.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a password locks the printer's menu. But it does not protect the drive itself; the depot can take the drive out and read the scans directly.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the printer will come back. But for two weeks the drive and its documents sit outside the office's control, so they still need protecting first.

tips: Eliminate: B locks the menu, which does not stop anyone reading the drive itself, and C ships the drive unprotected because the printer will return.
Final two: D beats A because deleting leaves the scans recoverable; sanitizing or removing the drive does not.
Exam cue: data leaves your control whenever the device does; deal with storage before repair, return or disposal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 MA-2 (Controlled Maintenance); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-08 (systems, hardware, software, services, and data are managed throughout their life cycles)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'devices sent for off-site repair have their storage sanitized or removed first' (notes 5.4.2 The Asset Lifecycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without 'and'/'record'; distractor B given 'or'. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded as 'X before Y', without the comma-ing tail; A (deleting) made the runner-up, the stronger trap (blind tester flag).

questions.question: After an approved patch, a photo lab's order system keeps crashing; the lab manager owns the system, but the change's rollback plan lets the on-call administrator undo failed patches. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Report the crashes to the lab manager and wait for a decision
options.B: Leave the patch and record each crash until the vendor's fix
options.C: Roll back the patch as the plan sets out and record it
options.D: Turn off the system's security settings until it runs

questions.key_concept: A change's approved rollback plan lets the assigned person undo a failed patch at once; it is recorded and the owner informed.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a change request's rollback plan is for.
questions.correct_explanation: The approved change already includes a rollback plan that lets the on-call administrator undo a failed patch, so restoring service is in role and needs no fresh approval. The administrator records it and tells the owner, since the flaw is open again and needs a new plan. Reporting to the lab manager and waiting is the runner-up: owners decide on their systems, but this decision was made when the rollback plan was approved.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the lab manager owns the system. But the approved rollback plan already gives the administrator this step, and waiting keeps orders down.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the patch closes a flaw. But a crashing system is an outage now, and recording crashes fixes nothing when an approved rollback exists.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a setting might be the cause. But disabling security settings creates new exposure outside any approved change, and may not stop the crashes.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps a broken system running on hope, and D weakens security through an unapproved change.
Final two: C beats A because the approved rollback plan already gives the administrator this step; the owner is told afterward.
Exam cue: a change's rollback plan is part of its approval; when a change fails, follow it, record it and inform the owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-2(3) (Baseline Configuration | Retention of Previous Configurations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an approved rollback plan lets the assigned administrator undo a failed patch' (notes 5.4.5 Patch Management). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A sailing school's system administrator has written a change request to update the booking server's firewall rules. Who should MOST appropriately approve it?

options.A: The administrator, as the approver who understands it best
options.B: A designated approver other than the person making it
options.C: The firewall vendor's support team, who know the product
options.D: The colleague who will help the administrator make it

questions.key_concept: Change approval comes from a designated person independent of the work, separating making a change from approving it.
questions.pre_read: Recall how change management separates duties.
questions.correct_explanation: Change management separates making a change from approving it: a designated approver, such as a change manager or board, reviews the risk, the test plan and the rollback plan, and is not doing the work. The colleague who will help make the change is the runner-up: they are a second person, but as part of the team carrying it out they are not independent of it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the administrator knows the change in detail. But approving your own change removes the independent check that catches mistakes and misuse.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor knows the product. But the vendor does not own the school's risk and has no authority to approve its changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the colleague is a second person. But they help make the change, so they are not independent of it; the approver must stand apart.

tips: Eliminate: A lets the requester approve their own change, and C hands approval to an outsider with no authority over the school's systems.
Final two: B beats D because a helper shares in making the change; approval comes from someone designated and independent of the work.
Exam cue: in change management, whoever makes a change does not approve it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'someone independent of the work approves a change' (notes 5.4.6 Change Management). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A cider maker's servers passed their secure baseline check at deployment two years ago and have not been checked since. Which approach should the system administrator propose as BEST?

options.A: Scan them against the secure baseline every month from now on
options.B: Leave them alone, relying on the check at deployment
options.C: Check them against the baseline after each security incident
options.D: Rebuild every server from scratch at the start of each year

questions.key_concept: Systems drift from their secure baseline over time, so regular scans compare them with it and catch changes early.
questions.pre_read: Recall what happens to configurations after deployment.
questions.correct_explanation: Updates, troubleshooting and quick fixes make systems drift from their baseline over time, so passing at deployment proves little two years later. Regular scans against the baseline catch drift, such as a disabled firewall, while it can still be corrected through the normal process. Checking after each incident is the runner-up: it does find drift, but only once an attacker may already have used it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the servers once met the baseline. But changes since then cause drift, and a two-year-old result says nothing about today's settings.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: post-incident checks do find drift. But they find it after an attacker may have used it; regular scans catch it first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a rebuild restores a clean state. But it disrupts service, and drift returns between rebuilds with nothing to detect it.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts a two-year-old result, and D swaps detection for disruptive yearly rebuilds that leave drift unseen in between.
Final two: A beats C because regular scans catch drift before it is exploited; post-incident checks find it after the damage.
Exam cue: baselines need ongoing checks; drift detection is regular, not a one-time pass at deployment.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-2 (Baseline Configuration); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-01 (configuration management practices are established and applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'regular scans against the baseline catch drift after deployment' (notes 5.4.4 Configuration Management and Secure Baselines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded ('every month'); distractor B without 'since'.

questions.question: A security analyst at a cold-storage warehouse finds that the PC sending its ammonia leak alerts to staff phones runs an unsupported operating system; the facilities manager owns it. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Switch the PC off until a supported replacement is installed
options.B: Upgrade the PC's operating system during tonight's closure
options.C: Leave it running and report the risk to the facilities manager
options.D: Disconnect it from the network and then tell the facilities manager

questions.key_concept: An unsupported system that protects people keeps running while its owner decides on replacement and compensating controls.
questions.pre_read: Recall the usual options for handling end-of-life systems.
questions.correct_explanation: The PC protects people: it warns staff of ammonia leaks, so keeping it working comes before the risk of its old operating system. The analyst leaves it running and reports to the owner, who decides on replacement and compensating controls and seeks any exception the policy requires. Disconnecting it is the runner-up: isolation often suits unsupported systems, but here it would stop leak alerts reaching phones, and it is not the analyst's change to make.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because an unsupported system cannot be patched. But switching it off silences leak alarms that protect people, and the decision belongs to the owner.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a supported system closes the gap. But an unplanned upgrade bypasses change management and could break the alarm software; it is the owner's call.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: isolation often reduces risk for unsupported systems. But this PC alerts phones over the network, so cutting it off silences warnings people rely on.

tips: Eliminate: A switches off a safety alarm, and B makes an unplanned upgrade that could break it; both act without the owner.
Final two: C beats D because disconnecting would stop leak alerts reaching staff; keep the safety system working and let the owner choose controls.
Exam cue: when a vulnerable system protects people, keep it working and report it; safety comes before the cyber fix.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-22 (Unsupported System Components); NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Section 2.4 (Comparing OT and IT System Security: human safety is paramount, followed by protection of the process)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an unsupported system that protects people keeps running while its owner decides' (notes 5.4.3 End-of-Life Software and Devices). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 5.5 Security testing. Test scope on shared premises
questions.question: During an authorized tailgating test of a food co-op's offices, the tester finds the door to another tenant's office, an accounting firm, propped open. What should the tester do FIRST?

options.A: Go in and photograph the office as evidence for the test
options.B: Ask an accounting firm employee for permission to go in
options.C: Go in through the open door briefly, touching nothing
options.D: Report the door to the sponsor without entering that office

questions.key_concept: Penetration testers act only within the written authorization and scope; anything outside it is noted, not explored.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a test's written authorization covers.
questions.correct_explanation: A test's authorization covers only the premises and systems its sponsor controls and agreed in scope. The accounting firm never authorized testing, so entering, even briefly, would be trespass, not testing. The tester stays out and reports the open door to the co-op, the test's sponsor, to raise with the building. Asking a firm employee is the runner-up: it sounds like permission, but a passing staff member cannot authorize a security test.
