wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the scan was clean. But scanners check for known software flaws; they do not try crafted prompts, so the chatbot's answers were never tested.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a clean scan feels complete. But a scan lists known flaws without exploiting them, while a penetration test shows what an attacker could achieve; neither replaces the other.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a server scan also tested the chatbot's answers, and B lets a clean scan replace a penetration test, which exploits weaknesses rather than listing them.
Final two: D beats C because model manipulation is not a software flaw that patching closes; the chatbot's AI behavior needs its own testing.
Exam cue: match the test to the risk. A clean scan covers known software flaws, not how an AI model responds to crafted input.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-5 (Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning); OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM01 (Prompt Injection: conduct adversarial testing and attack simulations, treating the model as an untrusted user)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a clean vulnerability scan says nothing about how an AI model handles crafted prompts' (notes 5.5.6 Testing AI-Integrated Defenses). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026. Final fix round (18 Nov 2026): options rebuilt as parallel scope claims with one shared opener, so the key is no longer the only cautious option (blind giveaway finding).

questions.subtopic: 5.3 Incident response. Signs found during routine work
questions.question: Working a slow-laptop ticket at a sailmaker, a help desk technician finds an unknown remote-access tool and a new admin account; procedure sends suspected incidents to the security team. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Uninstall the tool and delete the account, then tell the security team
options.B: Run a full antivirus scan and close the ticket if clean
options.C: Leave the laptop as found and alert the security team
options.D: Restart the laptop to see whether the tool starts again

questions.key_concept: Signs of intrusion found during routine support go to incident responders before anyone removes or restarts anything.
questions.pre_read: Decide whether this is still a repair job or now something else, and who handles that.
questions.correct_explanation: An unknown remote-access tool and a new admin account are signs of a possible intrusion, so the job moves from repair to incident handling, which the procedure gives to the security team. Leaving the laptop as found keeps evidence and lets responders scope the attack. Removing the tool and account first is the runner-up: it feels like fixing, but it destroys evidence and skips analysis of how far the attacker got.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the tool and account must go eventually, and the team does hear of it. But removing them first destroys evidence and skips analysis of other access.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a clean scan feels reassuring. But antivirus tools often miss legitimate remote-access software that attackers misuse, and closing the ticket hides a likely incident.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it looks like a quick check. But a restart wipes memory evidence, may trigger the attacker's tools, and delays the security team's response.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts a clean antivirus scan to rule out misused remote-access software, and D's restart wipes memory evidence.
Final two: C beats A because signs of intrusion go to the team the procedure names; removing traces first destroys evidence and skips scoping.
Exam cue: routine work that turns up signs of an attack stops being routine. Preserve what you found and hand it to incident responders.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-6 (Incident Reporting); NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Table 1 (Previous incident response life cycle model's phases and corresponding CSF 2.0 Functions)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'signs of intrusion found during routine work go to incident responders before anything is removed' (notes 5.3.2 The Incident Response Lifecycle and CSF 2.0). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A rope maker's incident response lead is planning its first ransomware tabletop exercise. What should the lead decide FIRST?

options.A: A scoring sheet that grades each participant's answers
options.B: The objectives, such as testing who may order isolation
options.C: A detailed scenario based on a recent ransomware news story
options.D: A live restore test to prove the backups work

questions.key_concept: An exercise starts from clear objectives, which then shape its scope, participants and scenario.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the other planning choices depend on.
questions.correct_explanation: Objectives come first because they decide everything else: who takes part, what the scenario must cover and how success is judged. An objective such as testing who may order systems isolated tells the team what the tabletop must test. A detailed news-based scenario is the runner-up: scenarios matter, but one written before the objectives may be vivid yet miss what the plan needs testing.

wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a realistic scenario keeps people engaged. But it is built to serve the objectives; written first, it may miss the decisions the exercise needs to test.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because results should be recorded. But a tabletop tests the plan, roles and decisions, not individuals; grading people discourages the open discussion that finds gaps.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because recovery matters. But a tabletop is a discussion and touches no systems; proving a restore needs a hands-on test, planned separately.

tips: Eliminate: A grades people when a tabletop tests the plan, and D asks a discussion exercise to prove a restore, which needs a hands-on test.
Final two: B beats C because objectives decide what the scenario must cover; a vivid scenario chosen first can miss the decisions that need testing.
Exam cue: plan any exercise from its objectives. Scope, participants and scenario all follow from what the exercise must show.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-84 Section 4 (Tabletop Exercises: discussion-based events); NIST SP 800-84 Section 4.2.3 (Identify the Objectives: tabletop objectives validate the plan's content, participants' roles and responsibilities, and interdependencies)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an exercise is planned from its objectives, which shape its scope, participants and scenario' (notes 5.3.7 Incident Response Exercises and Tabletops). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A plant breeder's research director, who owns its trial data, wants every new file labeled Restricted, the top level, to be safe, though most are routine schedules. Which response from the security analyst is BEST?

options.A: Label each new file Restricted, then review the levels yearly
options.B: Advise setting each file's level by the harm of its disclosure
options.C: Review each file's content and set its level on the director's behalf
options.D: Advise Internal labels, as trial data is rarely targeted

questions.key_concept: Classification levels follow the harm each item's disclosure would cause; marking everything top level wastes protection and weakens labels.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the classification levels are for, and what happens when everything gets the same one.
questions.correct_explanation: Levels exist to match protection to harm. Marking everything Restricted spends the strongest controls on routine files, slows work and teaches staff to ignore labels, so the analyst advises the director to classify each file by the harm its disclosure would cause; the director still decides. Labeling everything Restricted and reviewing yearly is the runner-up: a review would catch some errors, but a year of blanket top-level labels already defeats the scheme.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it follows the director's wish and adds a yearly check. But until then every file carries the top level, which wastes protection and teaches staff to ignore labels.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the analyst can read the files. But classification is the data owner's decision; security staff advise on levels and protect data, but do not set them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it avoids heavy controls. But advising a low level on a guess, without weighing harm, could leave valuable research exposed; the level must fit the data.

tips: Eliminate: C has the analyst set levels the data owner decides, and D lowers protection on a guess about who targets the data.
Final two: B beats A because levels should follow each file's harm from the start; a yearly review leaves a year of blanket over-labeling.
Exam cue: classification matches protection to harm. Too low exposes data; too high everywhere wastes controls and teaches people to ignore labels.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-2 (Security Categorization); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Information Owner/Steward)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'classification levels follow the harm of disclosure, so a blanket top level defeats the scheme' (notes 5.1.1 Data Classification and Labeling). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D5 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.
